articles.title: Long forgotten, OG 'dirty bomber' Jose Padilla is now free
articles.description: On November 16, four days after Jose Padilla was released from prison after serving 24 years, CNN, citing “seven US officials,” warned that Iran was planning to detonate “a so-called dirty bomb” in Washington, D.C. Do you remember the last time we heard overheated warnings about a “dirty bomb” attack? I do. In June 2002, I was contacted by Donna Newman and Andrew Patel, the attorneys representing Jose Padilla. This U.S. citizen, who converted to Islam in prison, joined al-Qaeda in 2001 and was arrested in Chicago. At the time of his capture, Attorney General John Ashcroft announced that “we have captured a known terrorist who was exploring a plan to build and explode a radiological dispersion device, or ‘dirty bomb,’ in the United States.” On June 9, 2002, President Bush ordered Secretary of Defense Donald Rumsfeld “ to detain Mr. Padilla as an enemy combatant .” Padilla was transferred to a military brig in South Carolina, and for the next 43 months he was interrogated, tortured , and held without charges. articles.title: Trump should court Chinese investment and make it work for us
articles.description: Throughout Boston, Massachusetts, elderly subway cars are slowly clacking along the tracks of “the T,” the city’s public transit mainstay. Renovations are progressing but have fallen well behind schedule. Slow-moving projects like this, alongside outages of Microsoft software, air traffic control systems, and banking, have left Americans around the country wondering about the strength of our infrastructure and tech development. How could the United States think differently about using investment and technology to deliver good outcomes? One answer might be found in Shenzhen, China, where the APEC Summit recently concluded. Last week, for the third time in six months, U.S. President Donald Trump met with Chinese President Xi Jinping, continuing an unprecedented pace of meetings. At APEC, Trump and Xi discussed trade, energy, artificial intelligence, fentanyl, and Taiwan. Concrete deliverables have yet to be announced, but the readouts proclaim productive conversations. articles.title: Court Rules Democrats' Proxy Voting Unconstitutional, Putting Other Biden-Era Laws In Question
articles.description: Court Rules Democrats' Proxy Voting Unconstitutional, Putting Other Biden-Era Laws In Question A federal appeals court ruled Friday that the House violated the Constitution when it relied on pandemic-era proxy voting to pass former President Joe Biden's $1.7 trillion spending package almost four years ago. Joe Biden, 2022. (Mandel Ngan/Getty) The Fifth U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in New Orleans split 9-8 in holding that the House lacked a constitutionally valid quorum when it approved the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023 in December 2022. The package cleared the chamber 225-201, according to the court's 58-page opinion. Of the members casting votes, 226 recorded both their votes and their presence by proxy , which left fewer than a majority of House members physically in the chamber. The majority concluded that the proxy arrangement violated Article I, Section 5 of the Constitution, which requires a majority of each chamber to form a quorum to do business. " 'Proxy presence' does not count ," Judge Cory Wilson, a Trump appointee, wrote for the majority. articles.title: Third Deputy Out: After Bongino And Bailey, FBI No. 2 Raia To Retire Days After Patel Skips Hearing
articles.description: Third Deputy Out: After Bongino And Bailey, FBI No. 2 Raia To Retire Days After Patel Skips Hearing The FBI's No. 2, Deputy Director Christopher Raia, plans to retire in December , three people familiar with his plans told the Washington Post on Monday. Hexbird, run by aviation data analyst John Wiseman, traced the roughly 20-minute burst of interference to a radio transmitter over the North Sea about 190 miles off the English coast. They included a Ryanair flight from Edinburgh to Rome, an easyJet flight from Manchester to Hurghada, Egypt, and a British Airways flight from London to Stockholm. articles.title: Michael Stone's 'performance art' attack on Stormont

But as politicians debated Stormont’s future, one former prisoner had other plans – Michael Stone. The footage of Stone trying to force his way into the Great Hall, throwing down a rucksack which he said had a 25lb bomb in it, was shown across the world. Stone later insisted the incident, over which he was convicted of attempting to murder Gerry Adams and Martin McGuinness, was “performance art”. Ciarán Dunbar is joined by the Executive Editor of Belfast Telegraph and Sunday Life Martin Breen and author and journalist Martin Dillon.

articles.title: After Eight: the story of Satpal Ram - documentary
articles.description: It is 40 years since a racially charged attack at a curry house led to Satpal Ram’s conviction for murder, but today Britain’s post-pub curry culture still has a dark side. Ram spent 24 years in prison before a global campaign for justice, led by bands including Asian Dub Foundation and Primal Scream, secured his release from prison. His case raises crucial questions about the UK’s ongoing struggle for racial equality Continue reading...

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto VI review – gaming’s most depraved world is now also its greatest love story
articles.description: With realism that defies belief, this vast game easily accommodates its trademark foulmouthed, OTT chaos – as well as new empathy for the fugitive couple at its centre Tell us: are you playing Grand Theft Auto VI? In GTA VI, Rockstar has created the most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world that we have yet seen. Reviewing it feels a bit like trying to review, say, Paris: it contains so many potential experiences that it’s hard to know where to start. If you had been spying on me playing this game over the past few weeks you may well have caught me robbing banks, shooting up a weed farm or tearing along the highway at sunset blaring Bad Bunny on the in-game radio, but you might equally have caught me doing squats at the gym, shopping, assembling a coffee table or walking along the beach eating ice-cream. There is such a multiplicity of things on offer here that it is difficult to nail down what this game definitively is. Is it an interactive crime movie? A city simulator? A driving game? A sort of absurdly expansive version of The Sims in which the people you’re dressing up and looking after just happen to be professional criminals? It will be different for everyone

articles.title: In a flap: how the butterfly became a symbol of gen Z resilience – and anxiety
articles.description: The delicate insect has become fashion’s favourite motif again – but having represented sexuality in the 90s and the soul in Greco-Roman times, what does it say about youth culture today? • Don’t get Fashion Statement delivered to your inbox? Sign up here In the new Gucci campaign, Mariah Carey blows a goodbye kiss to 2026 in the most Mariahhhh way possible. Dressed in a fake fur coat and an azure dress, she enters a Christmas party to the twinkly sounds of All I Want For Christmas Is You. There are beautiful people, presents wrapped with Gucci string and butterflies, which have been associated with the popstar since her 1997 album, Butterfly, but have recently fluttered back to become a symbol of gen Z defiance and girlhood. Carey serves as fairy godmother to the other “pop girlies” who have embraced the emblem, from PinkPantheress to Dua Lipa; Rachel Chinouriri to Marina and the Diamonds. At the Academy Museum gala in October, the singer Janelle Monáe looked as if she might take flight in a Robert Wun couture gown, with wide, yonic wings. Elsewhere, Tate McRae recently wore a black sequined butterfly bra and matching butterfly wing belt from lingerie wunderkind Ludovic de Saint S

We would like to hear from teachers about their experiences of seeing or being the victim of violence and abuse in schools, from either pupils or parents, within the last five years. What happened and was the incident reported? If the police were involved, what was the outcome? Please do not include any identifying details of the children involved. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘The greatest game ever made’: readers and Guardian staff on Grand Theft Auto VI
articles.description: Rockstar’s newest installment of its hit franchise still has plenty of action, along with a dose of ‘healthy masculinity’ Described as the biggest entertainment launch in history, the new Grand Theft Auto game has prompted avid fans around the world to take the day off work, stock up on snacks and celebrate its arrival after 13 years of waiting. While some have already spent hours immersed in the game’s criminal escapades, others have found themselves doing household chores, building houses or simply taking in the scenery – which includes more than 170 flora and fauna species native to Florida . GTA VI has generated extraordinary global anticipation for its action-packed gameplay, but players are now finding new delight in the game’s more intimate moments. Continue reading...

articles.title: Unreal deals: the scam websites targeting Black Friday bargain hunters

articles.title: Why I love Madrid in winter: ‘Locals get into the spirit by doing their shopping in novelty hats’
articles.description: The streets and squares of the Spanish capital come alive with Madrileños shopping, drinking and dining outdoors, warmed by lap blankets and patio heaters Live in Madrid long enough and you hear the same weather-related proverbs again and again. One old saying goes that the seasons in the Spanish capital break down to “nine months of winter and three months of hell”. And if the city never quite freezes over in the coldest months – except for the blizzard of the century that came with Storm Filomena in 2021 – it is also said that the subtle, evil wind coming in from the mountains could kill a person without snuffing a candle. Personally, I prefer it here at this time of year, though if you’re looking to escape the crowds you might be disappointed. Madrid has only got busier in the 11 years I’ve lived here, and Christmas feels more crowded than midsummer on the central streets around Puerta del Sol. All the main public squares get their own giant Christmas trees, while Plaza de España and Plaza Colón install ice rinks too, and a festive market fills the cobbled core of Plaza Mayor with painted wooden huts. articles.title: ‘I don’t blame any woman for being sucked in’: how the wellness industry is cynically exploiting menopause
articles.description: Where women see hot flushes and brain fog, pharmaceutical companies see dollar signs. But are products like lion’s mane mushrooms or even magnets for knickers really helping them? Or is it all just a big capitalist con? ‘Tequila?” says a woman brightly, proffering a pink plastic shot glass. It’s barely 10.30 on a Saturday morning, and my perimenopause wellness journey is not going entirely as expected. We are standing in a neon-lit London conference centre amid the hubbub of Pause Live , billed as the UK’s biggest annual women’s health and menopause event and essentially a consumer fair for those in midlife. All around me, women are sampling free squirts of menthol lotion (supposed to cool hot flushes) and paper thimblefuls of slightly grainy, sweet latte made with powdered Peruvian maca root instead of coffee. The tequila, it turns out, is a gift from the sponsors, with no miracle ingredients beyond alcohol. But stalls offer everything from neck creams to pelvic-floor trainers, mindfulness journals and hairpieces for disguising thinning locks, plus herbal supplements in every conceivable edible form: chocolate truffles, ginger shots, mushroom coffee. articles.title: Interpol and Bloc Party review – two of 00s indie’s most revered acts go toe-to-toe

Twelve months ago, when Interpol and Bloc Party announced a UK and European co-headline tour, the pairing looked like an even contest: two of 00s indie’s most revered acts, whose landmark debuts remain touchstones of the era. Since then, their fortunes have diverged. As an opening bass drone strafes the room, Bloc Party arrive in Cardiff in superficially fine, if puzzling, form. Their seventh album, Anatomy of a Brief Romance, has been met with diminishing returns, its Snapchat-caption triteness – “Every day is such a vibe”, runs one refrain – and creative inertia doing little to win over listeners. articles.title: ‘My name was poison’: Donny Osmond on fame, failure – and his friend Michael Jackson
articles.description: He was the child star of the Osmonds who become a global celebrity by 14. Then, at 21, his career came crashing down. Here, he reveals how he survived his years in exile – and what happened when Jackson was accused of child abuse For a brief period in the early 1970s, Donny Osmond ruled the world. He was the global teenage heart-throb. Even Michael Jackson trailed behind him. He was 14 when his most famous song, Puppy Love, spent five weeks at No 1 in the UK. My sister had a huge poster of him on her bedroom wall. Then again, everybody’s sister had a poster of him on their bedroom wall. Between 1972 and 1973 he had six Top 5 hits in the UK, three of them No 1s (including The Twelfth of Never and Young Love). He was equally successful back home in the US. Osmond was clean-cut, religious and respectful, with a mighty ability to punch out cover versions of saccharine standards. From his purple velvet cap to his doleful eyes and dazzling all-American smile, he was a marketing dream. We’d only just finished with Beatlemania. And now there was Donnymania. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘What if joining the resistance got your friends executed?’ The chilling new films casting Nazi collaborators in a fresh light
articles.description: For decades, films about Nazi-occupied Europe were all about the fearless resistance while despicable collaborators deserved all they got. So what’s behind the spate of movies portraying turncoats in a more sympathetic light? A young maid busies herself in a vast, high-ceilinged apartment, serving her master steaming coffee in fine china and polishing the hefty family silver, as she picks her way across the checkerboard parquet lit by stylish Poul Henningsen lamps. Woman Unknown , which won the Golden Lion at the Venice film festival this year, is set in the immediate aftermath of Denmark’s liberation from Nazi rule, but you wouldn’t know that from the opening scenes: five years of occupation, martial law and rationing have left the splendour of the Danish bourgeoisie miraculously untouched. The trauma of wartime violence only comes rushing back in occasional bursts: blurry flashbacks show shadowy figures pointing guns at temples and bodies thudding to the floor. But the red fabric billowing through the fog of her memory is not the Nazi flag but liberated Denmark’s white-crossed Dannebrog . articles.title: Why I love Berlin in winter: ‘Christmas markets arrive in a blaze of twinkling lights’
articles.description: The cold is legendary, but there’s hot chocolate and Glühwein to warm you up, plus crowd-free museums and galleries and cosy candlelit pubs One of the first things Berliners warned me about when I moved here in 2008 was the winters. They talked in hushed, conspiratorial tones about the harsh winds that blew in from the Russian steppes, temperatures of minus 15C and the horrors of frozen bike locks. Having survived 17 of these winters (and counting), and still no hospitalisations for frostbite to report, I can confirm that the warnings, although not necessarily untrue, are not the whole story. Although some Berlin winter days are cold, miserable and grey, they can also be charming, cheerful and chock-full of possibilities. No sooner has the temperature dropped, and the last yellow leaves see-sawed from the trees at the end of November, than the city’s Christmas markets assert themselves in a blaze of twinkling lights, aromatic grill smoke, candied nuts and warming cups of Glühwein. I think it’s disgusting. I think the people who run it are disgusting. They’ve made a massive gamble with humanity and society and culture.” His contempt may surprise anyone who’s familiar with Rankin’s substantial AI output. Ever since the artist Damien Hirst introduced him to the possibilities of generative AI in 2021, the British photographer has been going further down the rabbit hole. “I’m not somebody who likes to be critical about something without actually knowing about it,” he explains. “I’ve gone deep into trying to work it out.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Is it true that … we only use 10% of our brains?
articles.description: The idea that we access a fraction of our cognitive potential goes back decades, but does medical science agree? This idea really bugs Dr Mary Spiller , senior lecturer in the University of East London’s Department of Psychology and Human Development, who’s shocked by how prevalent it remains, despite being untrue. Spiller says the myth’s origins can partly be traced to the work of William James, one of the founders of modern psychology, working in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. He wrote: “We are making use of only a small part of our possible mental and physical resources.” Continue reading...

articles.title: The best Black Friday beauty deals I’d actually buy, from LED face masks to skincare staples
articles.description: We’ve rounded up the beauty and hair care offers that are actually worth it – all tried, tested and loved by us • The best Black Friday deals • The best Black Friday deals on winter essentials Few of us may be able to justify the cost of a big-ticket TV this Black Friday, but beauty is one area where we can usually afford a treat or two. Thank you, lipstick effect . It can feel like a no-brainer to stock up on our regular favourites and get a few Christmas presents crossed off the list while prices are lower. But deals do something funky to our brains. Retailers know how to lure us in, using big discounts and “selling fast” pop-ups that cause our typically rational brains to short circuit. Add a high-pressure countdown, and before you know it, you’ve been enticed into buying countless products you didn’t set out to buy. Impulse beauty buys are easy to regret later when you snap back into consciousness – not only because of the money you’ve spent, but also because of the waste they create. Continue reading...

articles.title: Will the Jilly Cooper plagiarism allegations taint our love of Rivals? I doubt it | Nadia Khomami
articles.description: The evidence seems overwhelming, but artists and writers have borrowed from each other for hundreds of years. The line between homage and theft is a thin one “Immature poets imitate; mature poets steal,” the poet TS Eliot wrote a century ago. No work of art, he argued, exists in a vacuum. Great writers draw on what came before them, transforming their influences into something entirely their own. Eliot’s words came to mind when I read the revelations about the queen of the country house bonkbuster Jilly Cooper, who has been accused of “extensive and deliberate” plagiarism in her 1978 book Prudence. At least 35 passages appear to have been lifted from The Serial, a satirical novel by American writer Cyra McFadden, alongside remarkable similarities to sections of Josephine Tey’s 1948 novel The Franchise Affair. McFadden’s daughter is threatening legal action, describing the treatment of her mother’s work as “unconscionable”. Nadia Khomami is arts and culture correspondent at the Guardian Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? articles.title: The Guardian view on Cop31: a just transition needs more than fine words | Editorial
articles.description: Petrostates blocked ambition while wealthy nations withheld cash support. The climate crisis demands the next UN summit turns promises into action In a negotiation the maxim is usually that no deal is better than a bad deal. But the failure of Cop31 in Turkey to get a climate pact – the first time this has happened in 17 years – should not be an excuse for leaving the planet with the damaging status quo. A hard bargain needs a credible route to agreement: by making commitments, seeking concessions and getting others to reciprocate. This did not happen at the weekend. Responsibility for the breakdown lay principally with petrostates resisting a transition away from fossil fuels and wealthy nations that are unwilling to finance it properly. With the US absent, the EU was foremost among the latter. European governments’ objection to fossil-fuel backsliding by a Saudi-Russian coalition was right, but they were wrong to rule out fresh EU funding for developing countries’ climate action. Despite their reservations, others – notably China and the African group – were prepared to accept a flawed package to keep multilateralism alive. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Guardian view on Andy Burnham’s EU intentions: undogmatic consensus building is a sensible strategy | Editorial
articles.description: On treacherous political terrain, the government is right to want to proceed with caution and at a pace of its own choosing During the 1980s and 90s, the French president of the European Commission, Jacques Delors, consciously pursued deeper EU integration via a gradualist approach that sought to minimise confrontation. Rather than focusing on ambitious end-goals, risking a showdown with some member states, Delors calculated that taking steps such as the creation of the internal market, in 1993, would eventually generate the momentum to go further. One thing would lead to another, in a logic of deeper union. Mindful of the unique capacity of the Brexit debate to divide and polarise, Andy Burnham appears, for the time being, to be adopting a version of this strategy. On Friday, the prime minister rightly hailed the signing of a reset deal with the EU on food exports, emissions trading and youth mobility as a “good day” for the UK. He then reiterated that further discussion was needed on finding the right long-term relationship with Brussels. Continue reading...

articles.title: Andy Burnham’s EU deal leaves Brexit open to question | Letters

Plus letters from Lindsay Bray , Helen Elliott and Nick Smith Your article ( Burnham seals trade and youth mobility deals in biggest step towards EU since Brexit, 20 November ) marks a welcome moment of political realism after years of denial about the consequences of Brexit. I wholeheartedly agree with Andy Burnham when he said: “This is a good day for Britain and this is a good day for Europe.” For years, the evidence has pointed in the same direction, that the UK economy is worse off as a result of Brexit. Trade barriers have increased, growth has suffered and businesses have been forced to navigate unnecessary bureaucracy. Many of the industries that Brexit supporters claimed would flourish have instead struggled. Fishing, farming, construction and touring musicians have all faced new obstacles, costs and restrictions. articles.title: A wake-up call for the UK government on wild birds | Letter
articles.description: Emma Phipps of SongBird Survival writes that the government must act now to save woodland and farmland species from extinction The Office for Environmental Protection’s finding that government departments are breaking the law by failing to protect wild birds should alarm us all ( UK government ‘breaking the law’ by not stopping decline of wild birds, 18 November ). The scale of bird declines in the UK is impossible to ignore, and songbirds are among the worst affected. The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs’ wild bird indicators show that nearly 70% of farmland songbird species have declined since 1970. Woodland songbirds are faring little better, with more than 30% of species in decline. Unfortunately, none of this comes as a surprise. Decades of monitoring by scientists and dedicated volunteers have shown that our wild birds are in trouble. Yet successive governments have failed to act with the urgency needed to halt these declines. Continue reading...

articles.title: If Trump, Xi and Putin are carving up the pudding, who gets the sixpence? | Letters
articles.description: Readers respond to an article by Rafael Behr on the Shenzhen summit, where the three world leaders met without a place at the table for Europe Rafael Behr ( Trump, Xi and Putin have a shared vision of global power – with no place for Europe, 18 November ) draws parallels between the Shenzhen summit and Winston Churchill, Joseph Stalin and Franklin D Roosevelt meeting at Yalta. I see it as bringing us a step closer to George Orwell’s Nineteen Eighty-Four, in which the world is divided into three superstates: Oceania, Eurasia and Eastasia. We already have the surveillance in the form of CCTV, facial-recognition technology and email trawling. Daily we witness the rewriting of history. We could be sleepwalking into a situation from which we will be unable to escape. Andy Fazakerley Irby, Wirral Continue reading...

articles.title: Sweden’s datacentre politics are more complicated than they appear | Letter
articles.description: There are distinct tensions over who controls, benefits from and gains access to natural and public resources, write James White and Nora Söderberg Steve Rose’s account of Sweden’s datacentre sector ( ‘Datacentres are deeply unpopular. Has Sweden made one we can all love?’, 12 November ) is a welcome reminder that digital infrastructure can be developed in more environmentally responsible ways. However, his suggestion that datacentres have become politically contentious elsewhere, “but here in Sweden, not so much”, is a misrepresentation. Consider the proposed Google datacentre development at Torsboda, near Sundsvall, which requires an enormous allocation of electricity and industrial land. The StoppaGoogle campaign , initiated by the regional political party Norrlandspartiet, has been vocal in challenging what this development will mean for electricity prices, employment and regional development. articles.title: Saariaho’s Adriana Mater transcends horror for hope. Female composers are rejecting opera’s legacy of violence | Annilese Miskimmon
articles.description: The death and pain of female characters has always been a bedrock of opera. Kaija Saariaho and today’s female composers are challenging this narrative, and thereby connecting with today’s world In 1992, the Finnish composer Kaija Saariaho saw a Salzburg festival production of Messiaen’s Saint François d’Assise. A series of meditative theological tableaux in which naturalism and plot is secondary to the revelation of deeper spiritual truths, it is now hailed as a masterpiece although it divided critics on its Paris premiere in 1983. Saariaho, one of the painfully few female composers in opera’s 400-year history, recalled thinking: “If that is an opera, then I can write one”. And she did, to notable international acclaim. Her first opera L’Amour de loin (Love from Afar), a tale of medieval courtly love with a libretto by war correspondent and writer Amin Maalouf was premiered, appropriately, at 2000’s Salzburg festival and came to the UK when English National Opera staged it in 2009 . articles.title: United Strings of Europe review – they’re the intersection in a Venn diagram of chamber music, string orchestra and jazz
articles.description: Wigmore Hall, London Centred around the world premiere of jazz bassist Misha Mullov-Abbado’s almost-concerto, the tight ensemble took a tour of classical fusion and tango fisticuffs In this eclectic programme of mostly 21st-century music, the United Strings of Europe found the intersection in a Venn diagram of chamber music, string orchestra and jazz. At its centre, receiving its world premiere, was The Travelling Violin by the jazz bassist and composer Misha Mullov-Abbado . In four movements, it’s an almost-concerto on an intimate scale. The solo violin, deftly played here by Tamsin Waley-Cohen, has the narrating role, but the writing for the nine supporting string instruments is so intricately woven that it feels like an ensemble piece. It almost seemed strange for Waley-Cohen to give a solo encore at the end, mesmerising though her playing of Nicola Matteis Jr’s A minor Fantasia was. Mullov-Abbado’s piece has a role for jazz bass, which he played himself, and for percussion, from soft-edged shimmering to driving, grooving drums, played by Fred Thomas; the jazz sensibility of both of these leaches into the rest. articles.title: The pet I’ll never forget: Susan Badger, the stray dog saved by a box of fried chicken
articles.description: No one could get close to this odd-looking pup when she appeared at a Maryland construction site. But hunger brought her in from the cold – and gave her a loving home I was driving to a doctor’s appointment in March when I saw a scruffy dog just sitting on the side of the Baltimore-Washington Parkway at a construction site, watching traffic go by. I noticed that she wasn’t wearing a collar. I thought to myself, that dog clearly doesn’t belong there – she needs help. Why is she out on her own? Workers at the construction site had built her a small shack, complete with a water bowl and food dish. Although she was spending some time there, whenever they would get too close she would run off. articles.title: Brioche armchairs, butter sculptures and edible chandeliers: meet the new food artists
articles.description: Culinary artists are turning fashion shows and design fairs into a feast for the eyes A pretty Venetian chandelier featuring delicate pink flowers and cascading blue leaves hangs from a ceiling. A hazy, warm light radiates from its tulip bulbs. Suddenly, a woman reaches up and snaps off one of the flower stems, giggling as she begins to nibble it. Welcome to the weird and wonderful world of Laila Gohar . The Egyptian-born, New York-based artist is part of a new wave of culinary artists blurring the lines between sustenance and spectacle, and this troupe have quickly become a firm fixture at fashion parties and design fairs, turning dining into a phenomenon and delight. Gohar describes the chandelier , made entirely from hand-spun sugar (including the silver chain that suspended it) as her “favourite thing she has done in recent history”. It joins a long list of extravagant yet still edible installations she has created, including lifesize armchairs made of brioche , an entire room constructed with Belgian chocolate and a four-metre-long mortadella that had to be lifted into the party’s venue using a crane. After he makes me a coffee and we sit at the square table, I feel obliged to raise the subject: aren’t we gonna cook something? “I thought we’d do some brunch,” he says. articles.description: The character comedian AKA Lee Nelson handed May a P45 and threw golf balls at Donald Trump. He explains why the pranking’s now on ice – and which funny footballers inspired him How did you get into comedy? I was booted out of every class for making jokes and then I discovered, at medical school, there is such a thing as a career in comedy. I was encouraged by being able to entertain the patients and went straight from that into comedy. Who did you admire when you were starting out? It was always the character comedians: Sacha Baron Cohen, Ricky Gervais, Steve Coogan. On the circuit Al Murray was doing the Pub Landlord. I admired anyone doing characters who could be dropped into multiple situations. As I started doing character comedy myself, I was inspired by people who might not have known how funny they were, such as a big batch of Premier League footballers from Beckham to Gerrard to Rooney. Simon Brodkin: Unleashed is at the Apollo, London , on 13 December and 11 March and on tour in the UK until 26 May Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘The numbers are very stark’: This primary school is the heart of a Welsh village. Can it be saved?
articles.description: Gladestry primary school is predicted to have only 19 pupils within two years, while its county council is forced to make cuts year after year. But residents still believe it’s worth fighting for The kitchen in the Alman family farmhouse is large, airy and decorated with hundreds of rosettes awarded over the decades for prize-winning dogs, sheep and cows. I grew up just up the hill, so I know this kitchen well. Apart from the video feed in the corner, showing what the cattle are up to in the barn, it hasn’t changed much since the 1980s when we’d pile in here after helping our fathers with the baling. From the kitchen, Gladestry’s small, slate-roofed primary school, set against the steep green slope of Hergest Ridge, is clearly visible, and – it being playtime when I visited – clearly audible too. That hasn’t changed much either since the days when Joseph Alman and I were pupils at that tiny school, and our own parents looked out of that same window and heard us calling to each other as we played football. Continue reading...

articles.title: You Can See Everything in Elizabeth Holmes’s unblinking eyes. Or can you? | Jason Okundaye
articles.description: The idea that seeing is believing is turned on its head in this documentary about the inscrutable Theranos founder, a world-class liar who may just be completely unreadable Warning: this article contains spoilers for You Can See Everything Elizabeth Holmes doesn’t believe that she’s ever told a lie. She “knows” that she hasn’t committed any crime. And she has no reason to deceive you. While speaking, she is gazing at her interviewer, Nathan Fielder, with those enormous, blue, vacant, unsettling, unblinking eyes. She doesn’t break eye contact. This is You Can See Everything, Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s documentary, which, at her invitation, follows Holmes and her husband, Billy Evans, at their home in San Diego in the weeks up to her surrender to custody at federal prison. Holmes is the disgraced tech ex-billionaire whose startup Theranos claimed the ability to run hundreds of comprehensive blood tests from a single pinprick of blood. This false claim posed “immediate jeopardy” to the health of thousands of patients and defrauded investors of more than $700m. Continue reading...

articles.title: Children of the revolution: how the north of England is defining modern men’s fashion
articles.description: Once the historic centre of the textile industry, the north is now home to a host of a provenance-driven labels. But is there a specific northern menswear look? And what does it all mean for the mad-fer-it stereotypes? In 2026, clothing has proved more important to Andy Burnham’s political identity than that of any British prime minister since Margaret Thatcher. He is a loyal Clarks and Adidas wearer, whose Howick worker’s jacket hangs in Manchester’s People’s History Museum. His ousting of Keir Starmer – launched shortly before being photographed jogging in a replica Everton shirt – has been memorialised as the “casual coup”. In one telling, the reason for this is simple: he’s a man from the north. That Burnham is the first born-and-bred northern male PM since Harold Wilson last swished his Gannex raincoat out of Downing Street goes some way to explaining his higher interest in clothing. It’s not necessarily that all men in the south care less about clothing, or that all men in the north do – but that many men from the north express it in such a distinctive, even unified, way. Continue reading...

articles.title: Cookie fever! How does Marks & Spencer knock out so many viral food sensations?
articles.description: Chicken kievs, ‘picky bits’, strawberry and cream sandwiches: the hits have been coming for almost half a century. Now Kathryn Turner, M&S’s head of product development, has become a social media celebrity. What’s the secret ingredient? The scenes in a Liverpool Marks & Spencer , after the release of the chain’s chocolate and cornflake cookie earlier this month, looked like brink-of-Covid panic buying crossed with a zombie apocalypse. It probably didn’t help that the baked goods hit the shelves at around the time the government started asking Britons to plan for an unnamed near-term disaster . How would we cope with a national emergency when we coped this badly with the crisis of not enough biscuits? You could explain the M&S cookie fever with reference to the company’s product development icon, Kathryn Turner, who has half a million followers between Instagram and TikTok, or the powerful urge to belong, in gen Z particularly. But it surely has something to do with the biscuit itself. As Rosie Sykes, the author of The Friday Biscuit, says: “Biscuits are very much part of the national fabric.” But lately they’ve had this “slightly weird glow-up”, gone “a bit max”, Sykes says. Whatev

articles.title: Council tax and stamp duty: both are a disaster zone. Scrap them and start from scratch | Polly Toynbee
articles.description: These ancient and often grossly unfair taxes are stifling the economy and young people. It’s long past time for radical reform When voters were asked in 2020 which tax they would cut first , council tax came out on top, and rightly so. Still, it’s taken six years for an array of Labour and Liberal Democrat MPs to call for reforms to this most grotesquely unjust tax. Prompted by a public petition organised by the campaign Fairer Share, a Westminster Hall debate heard calls for a review into property taxes, which would lay out options for replacing council tax and stamp duty land tax. Labour MPs were among those who have signed a letter to Downing Street calling for property tax reform to be a priority in Andy Burnham’s upcoming 10-year plan . Among flotillas of economists and thinktanks who signed the letter is Lord O’Neill, a Burnham adviser and former Goldman Sachs economist, who calls UK property taxation “utterly nonsensical”. Burnham has frequently backed reform of the “highly regressive” council tax and stamp duty, labelling them as “a tax on the aspiration of young people”. Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist Continue reading...

articles.title: Think you hate sprouts? Try these five recipes
articles.description: Chef Chantelle Nicholson says give them another chance smashed, pickled, smothered in cheese and breadcrumbs, or as fritters I have a confession to make: I have a sprout tattooed on my arm. It’s true. Such is my love for the small, green morsels of delight. If you don’t yet feel the love, then please give these a try – those memories of bitter, soggy and pallid balls of mush will be firmly shut in the past. So versatile are sprouts that they really do earn their place as a staple in the colder months; shredded, sauteed, roasted, fried or smashed, I urge you to find the joy! Continue reading...

Women had complained to the company’s management for years about the author’s alleged misconduct and harassment. The concerns raised included that Walliams had an “inappropriate” sexual relationship with a woman who was an intern when he first met her, had inappropriate interactions with at least three other women connected to the company including asking two for dates, and approached a girl who appeared to be in her teens at a book signing event. Within the first hour, checkpoints on the outskirts of the remote desert city nestled among the rocky hills of northern Mali had fallen to the insurgents, who pushed towards the police station where fierce fighting erupted. “Everything was happening at once. Explosions were going off all around us, people were shouting,” recalled a former member of Russia’s Africa Corps who was stationed in Mali at the time and spoke on condition of anonymity. “Nobody knew where the enemy was coming from.” Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘The lack of fun is as noticeable as the lack of content’: the reborn Museum of London is all piazza, no punch
articles.description: London Museum Smithfield Why has the revamped museum divided its exhibits into nonsensical themes and shunted all the fascinating stuff downstairs? The results are baffling, unengaging and soulless ‘ An astonishing sight’: Oliver Wainwright reviews the building’s architecture The Museum of London at the Barbican was the capital’s local museum, a crowded and quirky presentation of its history from the Dagenham idol to Vauxhall Pleasure Gardens . But apparently the location deterred casual visitors, and maybe it just wasn’t grand enough to reflect London’s self-conscious significance. For not since ancient Rome has a capital dominated its nation’s history and culture like London. So now we get the rebranded and reimagined London Museum Smithfield. History surrounds you in this neighbourhood: Black Death burials by the Charterhouse, the Knights of St John, the Smithfield martyrs, William Wallace’s execution site. So goodbye scruffy brutalist Slough House location, hello deep history. Except when you enter the new museum, all that history, all those layers going back to the Romans and earlier, have been brushed away. If you want an illustration that bigger is not better, this is it. Wh

articles.title: You Can See Everything’s chaotic battle for the narrative about Elizabeth Holmes
articles.description: In Nathan Fielder’s new documentary, the protagonists and film-makers battle over who is the hero and who is the villain. It’s a fascinating insight into modern celebrity promotion • Don’t get the Close Up delivered to your inbox? Sign up here Thank you for signing up to the Close Up newsletter. This is our first-ever edition! And, just like on the show , I’ll be zooming in on the big culture questions and recommending things I’m obsessed with. I’ll also give you a sneak peek of what’s coming up on the show and what the team have been talking about behind the scenes. OK, I’ll admit it: I wanted to hate You Can See Everything, the A24 documentary about Theranos fraudster Elizabeth Holmes, which finally arrived in UK cinemas last week. The marketing was slick, the hype was unparalleled. I didn’t believe a three-hour documentary about a disgraced tech CEO could be that good. But, like our colleague Adrian and basically every film critic who’s seen it, I left the cinema thinking: that was amazing and what on earth did I just watch? Continue reading...

articles.title: Hexed review – Disney’s witchy caper is a wicked disappointment
articles.description: A teen girl discovers she is a witch in this mostly magic-free reminder that original animation is stuck in an unoriginal place As bleak as Disney’s overreliance on sequels might have become, it’s not quite as bleak as the crumbling state of its original output. Obviously because of the former, the latter category has become that much less populated but even when the studio has recently bothered to release something without a number in the title, it’s been hard to really see the point. With or without Pixar, films like Elio, Strange World, Raya and the Last Dragon, Luca, Elemental, Onward and Wish have all felt as uninspired as something a rival might try to desperately cobble together in an attempt to lure kids away from Disney. Three Thanksgivings ago, Wish was a particularly poor yet extremely smug example of how rubbishy things have got, a personality-free princess tale that doubled up as a 100-year anniversary victory lap. It was Disney’s worst-reviewed animated film in almost two decades and its deserved box office failure cost about $131m. Unperturbed, its co-director Fawn Veerasunthorn (along with Moana 2 director Jason Hand) is back this holiday with another rote rip-off a

articles.title: ‘The Terence Conran of his day’: the visionary Victorian futurist adored by design superstars today
articles.description: A professor at the age of 21, Christopher Dresser was a design genius who created beautiful, futuristic homeware, from teapots to toast racks to jugs. Why is his brilliance only now being recognised? Victorian industrial designer Christopher Dresser was always a visionary. As a child, he was so artistically gifted he went to design school in 1847 when he was just 13. He became a professor at 21, dreaming up theories based on plant structure that changed the way designers worked. But it was after he quit academia that he really started to break boundaries. As a self-declared “design doctor”, he experimented with production techniques that brought beautiful, futuristic homeware into everyday houses. He was one of the first western designers to travel to Japan, helping introduce Japonisme to British life, which has had a transformative effect on furniture and decoration ever since. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Royal Court’s new mission? To boldly go back to the 60s space race with The Afronauts
articles.description: Royal Court theatre, London Ryan Calais Cameron’s ‘true(ish)’ account of a charismatic freedom fighter’s plan to take a Zambian crew to the moon never quite lifts off Ryan Calais Cameron has proved himself a playwright of stratospheric talent. His previous plays For Black Boys Who Have Considered Suicide When the Hue Gets Too Heavy and Retrograde both streaked their way into the West End. This new one is filled with mighty ambition but does not lift off in the same way. It is based on what he calls a “true(ish)” story. The figure of Edward Mukuka Nkoloso (Lucian Msamati) is taken from Zambian history. A freedom fighter for the nation’s independence in the 1960s, he set up a national academy for science and trained a group of “afronauts” in the hope of beating the US and the Soviet Union in the race to reach the moon. Nkoloso, a kind of Dead Poets Society inspiration figure here, picks 17-year-old Martha (Ama Qamata) for the mission. Continue reading...

articles.title: I don’t have children. A stranger decided I was ruining my life
articles.description: A reader sent me unsolicited photos of his children, insisting I was missing out on everything. Why are other people’s reproductive choices so threatening to many of us? Last fall, a man I had never met wrote to inform me that my fertility window was “rapidly closing” – and that I couldn’t possibly be happy. What had prompted this unsolicited assessment was an article I had published about how fascist regimes seek to control women’s roles in society. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘An extravagantly illuminated beast’: the best artificial Christmas trees in the UK – tested
articles.description: Pick wisely, and your fake fir could be reused for decades of Decembers. From pre-lit to frosted to space-saving, here are our festive favourites • The best beauty Advent calendars • The best Christmas baubles In the 70s and 80s Essex of my youth, no one had a real Christmas tree unless they lived in the country, or perhaps Loughton. Our family’s skinny artificial tree is now 55 years old and comes out every year at my sister’s. It’s shed a few plastic “needles” down the years, but it’s still standing proud – which is more than you can say for a real Christmas tree bought in 1971, or even 2025. Therein lies the surprising environmental efficiency of artificial Christmas trees. The Carbon Trust says using a fake tree over seven to 20 years (depending on its weight and materials) can create fewer emissions than buying a new, commercially grown tree every year. The key is to buy an artificial tree you’ll love enough to roll out for decades. Continue reading...

articles.title: Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia is elite impunity | Moira Donegan
articles.description: After the CEO was reinstated after Trump’s pressure campaign, it is abundantly clear: there are different rules for rich people There are different rules for rich people. If you or I acted the way that Jensen Huang has been accused of acting – allegedly berating and mistreating employees, sleeping with subordinates, and seeming to carry on a staggering number of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman identified by US intelligence as a likely Chinese spy who helped smuggle the company’s product to China – we probably would find ourselves out of work and out of favor for quite some time. But this is not so for Huang, the tech founder and close ally to Donald Trump who was recently ousted from Nvidia, the chip manufacturer he founded. On Monday, after a pressure campaign from Donald Trump, JD Vance and other members of the Trump administration, Huang was reinstated as CEO by the Nvidia board. Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnist Continue reading...

articles.title: Mariella Frostrup calls AJ Odudu ‘aggressive’ – and here we go again. We tire of this angry black woman trope | Natalie Morris
articles.description: Microaggressions pile up, and then they are triggering. Amid the latest row on I’m a Celebrity, we’re obliged to explain this hurt all over again When I heard Mariella Frostrup call AJ Odudu “aggressive” over the weekend on I’m a Celebrity … Get Me Out of Here!, my heart sank with sick recognition. For her part, AJ’s mother has since said that watching her daughter experience this all-too-familiar dynamic was a “living hell”. I know many Black women tuning in will have felt a collective shudder of disgust and solidarity. Of course, there is pushback. “Our addiction to offence is tearing us apart,” wrote a Telegraph pundit on Monday . But, this language is not neutral. There is a long history of Black women having their conduct and tone disproportionately scrutinised by white people. And what happened between Odudu and Frostrup is a tale as old as time. A Black woman stands up for herself and, no matter how reasonably she presents her argument, she is accused of aggression. It is an efficient tactic to flip the focus on to the behaviour of the Black woman, and it is rooted in racist stereotypes. Natalie Morris is the author of Mixed/Other: Explorations of Multiraciality in Modern Br

articles.title: Why the genocide verdict against Myanmar has big implications for Israel | Geoffrey Robertson
articles.description: Proving the ‘crime of crimes’ against an individual is notoriously difficult, but the ICJ has set a precedent for states to be found liable. Israel could be next For the first time ever, a state has been found guilty of genocide – that “crime of crimes” – and has been ordered to compensate victims and to prosecute and punish the perpetrators. This judgment came from the international court of justice (ICJ), which has convicted Myanmar of killing and expelling many thousands of Rohingyas in Rakhine state in 2017 . The court did not change the definition of the crime, settled by the genocide convention in 1948 as requiring proof of an intention to destroy, in whole or part, a racial or religious group as such. But it made the prospect of proving this against a nation a good deal easier than against an individual. It set a precedent for its next case concerning state liability, namely the case brought by South Africa against Israel. Geoffrey Robertson KC was a UN appeal judge and is author of World of War Crimes – Eyeless in Gaza and Beyond Continue reading...

articles.title: Compass’s logic for US listing is flimsy but UK ministers need to wake up to Footsie flight risk | Nils Pratley
articles.description: The contract caterer switching to New York is a big hit to the London Stock Exchange but what is being done to discourage others from delisting? That’s gratitude, eh? Compass Group built its business, in part, on contracts to serve dinners in British schools and run catering operations in NHS hospitals. Now it plans to switch its primary stock market listing to New York in 2028. Compass is a bad one for the London market to lose. First, it is the 18th largest company in the FTSE 100 index and one of the few that is the biggest in the world in its market (contract catering, not just for the public sector but for thousands of corporate clients). Second, its reasons for joining the stateside listing rush feel flimsy – but also dangerous. Continue reading...

articles.title: $150 for photos of Melania looking like a waxwork? Will the Trumps ever run out of money-making ideas? | Arwa Mahdawi
articles.description: From the first lady’s Amazon documentary to Barron’s energy drink, the family is raking it in during Donald’s second term. And that includes the president Melania Trump is not a regular mom. She’s “a very cool mom”. We know this because she says so in her very cool new TV docuseries , which no one asked for, but which Amazon made anyway. I should clarify that Melania: The Series is not to be confused with Melania, the 104-minute-long $75m (£57m) movie Amazon released earlier this year. You know, the one an industry insider called “the most expensive documentary ever made that didn’t involve music licensing”. Various people insinuated nasty things about alleged corruption when that film came out, but I think it’s sweet how patriotic Amazon seems to be. While our cup may runneth over with Melania content, I have good news for first lady fans. We’ve been graced with even more Melania merch. At the weekend, Melania announced an “exclusive collection of digital photographs by internationally acclaimed photographer Ellen von Unwerth” to complement her new docuseries. For the non-refundable price of $150 (£115) you get one black-and-white digital image of the first lady sitting on a chair

articles.title: The Ukraine-Russia war is escalating – and it will go global unless Europe speaks with one voice | Simon Tisdall
articles.description: Attacks from the Mediterranean to eastern Europe to the Baltic Sea are a rebuke to western complacency. Trump is a liability, and he must be bypassed to ensure peace Ukraine’s spectacularly successful weekend drone attack on a spanking new Russian warship docked in the Libyan port city of Benghazi, more than 1,300 miles (2,200km) from Kyiv, is further proof, if it were needed, that the catastrophic full-scale war Vladimir Putin launched in 2022 is escalating and spreading uncontrollably. The sinking follows a similar incident in the Baltic last week, which crippled a Russian cargo ship, and previous Ukrainian attacks on oil tankers and Russian navy ships and bases in the Black Sea region. Last week, Russia was blamed for a missile and drone strike on Nato member Poland , which Donald Tusk, the Polish prime minister, claimed was intentional, and for deliberately targeting western diplomatic compounds in Kyiv. While Moscow’s murderous winter bombing of Ukrainian civilians and energy infrastructure continues apace, provocative and disruptive Russian hybrid warfare operations across all of Europe, including sabotage, arson and cyber-attacks, are becoming daily occurrences. Simon Tisdal

articles.title: Senegal restored as Africa Cup of Nations champions after court ruling
articles.description: Senegal won January’s final 1-0 after walking off Result was overturned in March as 3-0 win for Morocco Senegal have been reinstated as the champions of Africa, and their controversial 1-0 victory over Morocco confirmed in the record books, after the scandal over January’s Africa Cup of Nations final was resolved in a Swiss courtroom. articles.description: Youngest title match in chess history starts Tuesday Sindarov and Gukesh open Game 1 with Berlin defense Explainer: all your pre-match questions, answered Preview: Gukesh vows to win title ‘all over again’ Sindarov interview: ‘I can’t play games just for fun’ Play through 22 famous world championship games Bluesky Bryan at @BryanAGraham or email him The players have shaken hands and we’re off! articles.description: Mauricio Pochettino said after game it was ‘never a foul’ Player now eligible to face Brentford on Saturday Manchester United have successfully appealed against the decision to send off Leny Yoro in their 4-0 defeat to Liverpool. articles.title: Salt and Donald vaporise target as England crush Australia in 13.1 overs to win second T20
articles.description: “Two proud Welshmen ticking a box for the England and Wales Cricket Board,” is how a beaming Aneurin Donald jokingly put it. articles.title: ‘I’m loving it at Brugge’: Freddie Potts on going from West Ham’s bench to Champions League
articles.description: Midfielder is preparing to face Liverpool after leaving the club he loves and overcoming a tough start in Belgium In April Freddie Potts was absorbing the disappointment of being substituted at half-time during West Ham’s FA Cup quarter-final defeat by Leeds. The midfielder was out of favour under Nuno Espírito Santo and could not have imagined that he would be preparing to face Liverpool in the Champions League seven months later. It is the 23-year-old’s reward for taking the difficult decision to leave his boyhood club last summer. Potts noticed his minutes were drying up in pre-season, even though West Ham were not exactly stocked with talent after relegation, and was ready for a new challenge when Club Brugge offered about £10m to sign him. Continue reading...

articles.title: Barnet footballer Isiah Noel-Williams charged with three counts of rape
articles.description: Noel-Williams remanded in custody by police Charges also include count of assault by penetration A League Two footballer has been charged with three counts of rape and remanded in custody by Hertfordshire police. articles.title: The Breakdown | North v south: who makes the cut in our fantasy XVs for a hemisphere head-to-head?
articles.description: Before the Nations Championship finale, picking MVPs for all-star hemisphere teams plus a global XV is far from easy This week the world’s top 400 rugby players will be assembling in the same city . You can only hope London’s steak restaurants and cafes are braced for the simultaneous influx of an army of huge men with even larger appetites. If tall buildings start to sway in the Twickenham area, you will know the buildup to this weekend’s Nations Championship finals is intensifying. Which begs a timely question. With this week billed as a north v south duel – there is even a trophy on offer to the champion hemisphere – it is not a bad moment to sit down with pen and paper and play fantasy selector. articles.title: Outcry grows over Labour plan to exempt most brownfield sites from nature protection rules
articles.description: Chancellor’s decision to exempt plots up to 1.5 hectares allows developers to dodge rules aiming to reverse wildlife declines An outcry is growing over the UK chancellor’s removal of most brownfield housing plots from a legal requirement for developers to measurably enhance nature. John Healey’s decision in the budget to exempt brownfield plots of up to 1.5 hectares from biodiversity net gain (BNG) laws effectively means housing developers of inner-city, urban and surburban sites will be able to dodge rules designed to reverse steep wildlife declines while also allowing housebuilding growth. According to government data, 86% of brownfield sites currently registered are 1.5ha or under. Continue reading...

articles.title: Prisoner given second whole-life term for murdering Soham killer Ian Huntley
articles.description: Anthony Russell attacked Huntley with a metal bar while they were in a recycling workshop at HMP Frankland A prisoner who bludgeoned the Soham killer Ian Huntley to death with a 4kg metal bar has been sentenced to a second whole-life term. Anthony Russell was already serving a whole-life order for three murders. On Tuesday, he pleaded guilty to the murder of Huntley and was given the same sentence. Continue reading...

articles.title: Trump expected to award Giuliani Presidential Medal of Freedom
articles.description: Trump’s former lawyer was disbarred for his efforts to help the US president overturn 2020 election results Donald Trump is expected to present Rudy Giuliani, his former personal attorney who was disbarred for his efforts to help the US president overturn 2020 election results , with the Presidential Medal of Freedom on Tuesday. articles.title: Gaza issues meningitis epidemic alert after steep rise in cases
articles.description: Health ministry records 272 new infections in October, more than eight times the normal monthly rate Gaza’s health ministry has issued an epidemic alert after a sharp rise in meningitis infections, with more than 270 new cases reported in October. Dr Nidal Ghoneim, a senior official at the ministry, said the spread of the disease posed a threat to the lives of hundreds of thousands of people, including children. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Menacing eyes’: Pope Francis’s diary details three encounters with the devil
articles.description: Late pontiff’s innermost thoughts, reflections and fears are revealed in published passages from his private diary Pope Francis wrote in his diary of encountering the devil and said he saw the “gates of hell” when he realised how serious a clerical sexual abuse scandal was, according to excerpts published on Tuesday. articles.title: Summer heat deaths in 2026 reached record high of 5,258 in England
articles.description: Figure for May to September is far higher than previous peak of 2,985 since records began a decade ago More than 5,200 deaths in England in 2026 were linked to summer heat, the highest provisional annual total since records began a decade ago, according to the UK Health Security Agency. The government agency said 5,258 deaths were associated with extreme heat between May and September 2026. Continue reading...

articles.title: Their loss changed Appalachian forests for ever. Now the American chestnut is back
articles.description: The trees have been functionally extinct in the US for nearly a century. But new techniques are creating plants resistant to the parasitic blight that almost wiped them out Jeff White is starstruck by a tree. The farmer and environmentalist from rural Maryland has an affinity with the American chestnut but has never seen one stretch from root to sky like this one. “About how tall is it?” he asks. “Over 70ft [21 metres],” says Cassie Stark, director of science implementation for the American Chestnut Foundation (TACF). “Just incredible,” White says, his gaze fixed upwards. “I’ve never seen one so tall and so healthy.” ‘Thompson’, above left, is an unusually tall specimen of an American chestnut, a now-rare species once ubiquitous in the US. Jeff White next to ‘Gladys’, a thriving 15-metre-tall pure American Chestnut in Virginia’s Lesesne forest Continue reading...

articles.title: Justice system failing crime victims ‘at every point’, ministers told
articles.description: Without reform there will soon be ‘no point’ in the public reporting crimes to the police, says victims’ commissioner for England and Wales There will soon be “no point” in the public reporting crimes to the police, the victims commissioner for England and Wales has said, as she urged ministers to reform the justice system. Claire Waxman called on Andy Burnham to put reforming the justice system at the heart of his 10-year plan for government, expected to be unveiled next month, because victims were being failed “at every point”. articles.title: After 80 years in Oxford, Naga ancestors are finally going home
articles.description: A campaign securing the landmark return to India of ancestral remains taken during British colonial rule has opened a wider conversation about restitution • Don’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up here The lacerating legacy of colonialism survives in many spaces, particularly in museum collections and private holdings across the western world. And it’s not just limited to inanimate artefacts or cultural objects. articles.title: Under-16s social media ban could disrupt sites that pose no risk, says UK tech industry
articles.description: Trade body techUK says regulations are causing frustration with chaotic process of ‘chasing children around the internet’ A large expansion of the social media ban for teenagers has been a chaotic process of “chasing children around the internet” and could disrupt websites that pose no risk, the head of the UK’s tech trade association has said. articles.title: Meta launches Muse in UK – the AI agent that can do your Christmas shopping

articles.title: ‘The icing on the cake’: how Nigella saved Bake Off
articles.description: Viewing figures are up and the new judge has spiced up the show with her wit, charm and articulate appreciation of doughy delights. The stale previous seasons are fast becoming a mere memory When Nigella Lawson helps crown the new champion of The Great British Bake Off on Tuesday night, two other winners will also be celebrating: the show itself and broadcaster Channel 4. The fabled “Nigella effect” has freshened up a franchise that was beginning to taste distinctly stale. Having replaced Prue Leith as judge for this 17th edition, alongside the ever-present Paul Hollywood, the domestic goddess has made the cake-making contest essential viewing again. Prompting a public outpouring of love, magisterial Lawson has proved the missing ingredient in the show’s resurgence. Continue reading...

articles.title: Scream 4 came out 15 years ago – but its mockery of online brainrot is more spot-on than ever
articles.description: When Wes Craven’s final slasher film came out, correctly predicting clout-chasing influencers and social media’s corruption of our lives, Instagram was just six months old Get our weekend culture and lifestyle email It has been almost a year since Australia’s social media ban for under-16s and it seems as though nothing has been able to effectively deter the youth from the slippery slope of internet addiction – even when they have expressed the desire to quit . It’s hard to believe that it has only been a decade since TikTok condemned us to the eternal doomscroll and just over 15 years since Instagram launched. Surely no one predicted just how much the online world would be leeching off of us, right? Well, Wes Craven did. Craven is the mind behind notable horror titles including The Hills Have Eyes, A Nightmare on Elm Street and the Scream franchise – and the last film he directed, four years before his death in 2015, was Scream 4. Continue reading...

articles.title: The World of Love review – beautifully directed and compellingly elusive family mystery
articles.description: Yoon Ga-eun’s film tracks the uneasy fallout after a teenage schoolgirl makes a deeply shocking announcement to her class Korean film-maker Yoon Ga-eun creates a strange world of bewilderment, sadness and pain – but not much of love – in this involving and mysterious family drama. It seems always to be gesturing at an indefinable sense of loss, a poignant keynote struck by the recurring soundtrack piano arrangement of Bach’s Sheep May Safely Graze. Seo Su-bin gives an excellent performance as Joo-in, a high schooler possessed of a cheeky, madcap sense of fun, like her wacky, magic-obsessed kid brother Hae-in (Lee Jae-hee). She is keen on taekwondo and often shown (in borderline-uncomfortable closeup) kissing boyfriends that she will later dump. But when classmate Su-ho (Kim Jeong-sik) asks her to sign a petition objecting to the release and local rehousing of a convicted child rapist, Joo-in refuses, on the ostensible grounds that the petition talks about the permanent damage done to rape victims. Joo-in astonishes and upsets the class by announcing at the top of her voice that she herself is a rape victim, and she has not been permanently damaged – and then says it was just a joke

articles.title: To Hold a Mountain review – a spectacular setting for tough savvy woman’s fight against the government
articles.description: A livestock farmer with a sad secret in her past rallies to keep military training out of her breathtaking mountain home in Montenegro An award-winner in Sundance, where it premiered earlier this year, this slow-burn documentary follows a middle-aged Montenegrin livestock farmer called Gara and her 13-year-old daughter Nada. The two of them eke out a hardscrabble living on Sinjajevina, a breathtaking mountain plateau on which Montenegro’s government would like to conduct training exercises for its own army as well as Nato’s. This goes down about as well as a wolf in the sheep pen with flinty Gara, who rallies her neighbours as well as the local media to fight the proposal. She displays a savviness that’s somewhat surprising, even if her fortitude and strength of conviction seem completely in character. However, that fight against the state is just one element of a film that, through long, languid takes, reveals the women’s stately pastoral existence, one taken up above all with care for their menagerie of animals (cows, sheep, goats, cats and dogs) and each other. Co-directors Petar Glomazić and Biljana Tutorov gradually reveal the family setup isn’t exactly what it appears at firs

articles.title: Sir Stanley Wells obituary
articles.description: Eminent Shakespeare scholar and author who brought together the worlds of academia and the theatre In 1978 Oxford University Press made Stanley Wells, who has died aged 96, director of a Shakespeare department specially created so that he could produce a new edition of the complete works. Starting from scratch, he went back to the early printed copies, the quartos and folios, and thought through every editorial and textual decision – how to modernise the spelling and punctuation, and edit stage directions and speakers’ names, while giving the rationales for emendations. The single volume Complete Shakespeare appeared in 1986, edited by Stanley, with Gary Taylor, John Jowett and William Montgomery. It proved to be groundbreaking, startling and controversial. Continue reading...

articles.title: From Sovereigns to Servants by Alexandra Prokopenko review – Putin and his yes men
articles.description: A disturbing account of the way Russia’s elites have reduced themselves to craven courtiers When Vladimir Putin launched his full-scale invasion of Ukraine four and a half years ago, it was a shock, but it wasn’t a surprise. The US and the UK had been publicly warning their allies for weeks about what Russia was planning, as well as threatening the Russians with a wave of sanctions unprecedented against a major power. Putin’s foreign policy had long relied on confusion and untruth. By saying that they knew exactly what he was up to, Britain and America were hoping first to deny him his usual ambiguity, and second to pressure the men around him into making him stop, since war would deprive them of the stolen assets they’d stashed in London’s most exclusive neighbourhoods. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Song of Stork and Dromedary by Anjet Daanje review – don’t miss this glorious epic inspired by Emily Brontë
articles.description: The afterlife of a Yorkshire village girl who becomes a gothic literary icon is explored across three centuries, in a thrilling paean to the power of books I had a plan. I was going to nibble away at this great wedge of a book, a morsel a night, like a little reading mouse. But then the story swallowed me whole. I read Dutch author Anjet Daanje’s The Song of Stork and Dromedary over three feverish nights, and spent the days in between longing for the dark. This 720-page novel should come with a warning label: may cause severe infatuation. We begin in the fictional Yorkshire village of Bridge Fowling with Susan Knowles-Chester, a woman who attends to the dead. The year is 1847, and Susan knows the old ways, the threshold rituals: how to arrange a corpse so it doesn’t gape and gawp at the living. “The villagers have a horror of her work, for wherever she goes, she leaves grief like driftwood in her wake, yet when the time comes, many ask for her help, it is an open secret.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Man Theft Auto – why did so few women review GTA VI, the biggest video game of the decade?
articles.description: Given that this is the first Grand Theft Auto in 30 years with a female protagonist, you might have expected to hear from female critics. But you would have expected mostly in vain Grand Theft Auto VI is now the biggest video game launch of all time, and is likely to become the biggest video game of all time. It’s a once-in-a-lifetime event, a phenomenon that will shape games as a medium and pop culture at large for years to come, set against the backdrop of its developers fighting for their rights at studio Rockstar Games . It has snatched sales and streaming records and become the best-reviewed game ever (pulling ahead of 1998’s The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time). It’s also the first GTA game with a female protagonist, who also happens to be a woman of colour. Yet very few women (and seemingly no women of colour) played and reviewed it before release. When GTA VI’s review embargo lifted on 18 November, the gender imbalance was immediately obvious. Out of 156 reviewers, only six appeared to be women. As journalist Lex Luddy noted in a BlueSky post , that is 3.8%. Continue reading...

articles.title: GTA VI’s jaw-dropping success: in figures
articles.description: Content creators have produced hundreds of millions of hours of video game since its launch Grand Theft Auto ( GTA) VI became the largest video game release of all time last week and while it is hard to say exactly how many people are playing the game (current estimates say at least 30 million), there are plenty of other jaw-dropping data points we do know. Data on streaming the game suggests that only two days into its release a cumulative 364.5m hours have been watched – roughly 41,000 years of content. Put another way, that translates to more than 41,000 years worth of people riffling through cash registers, hanging drywall, birding, diving or hijacking jets. That’s according to streaming data from Streams Charts, a data and analytics company that has been tracking Rockstar Game’s long-awaited title. Continue reading...

articles.title: What happened when the man who took a million photographs embraced colour?
articles.description: The Photographers’ Gallery, London Sanlé Sory is known for his black and white images taken during independence in Burkina Faso – but his colour portraits bring humour, insouciance and joy Despite his wide renown, there have been hardly any major exhibitions of Sanlé Sory’s work. His last UK show was in 2019, concentrating on the black-and-white images the Burkinabé photographer made in the first two decades after opening his own studio, Volta Photo, in Bobo-Dioulasso in 1960 – a period that coincided with the first two decades of independence in Burkina Faso. This new Photographer’s Gallery show shifts the focus to the 1980s and 1990s, when Sory began working in colour. It’s easy to see why, even with few exhibitions, Sory has made such an impression on audiences. There are the familiar west African studio photography tropes westerners love, where sound, image, fashion and pose collide. The props are popping, the style is irrepressible, the energy is irresistible. I wonder if Sory’s speed and instinct came from the time he spent early in his career racing on his motorbike to photograph car accidents for newspapers and the police. These portraits are the opposite of a car crash, th

articles.title: RPO/Hisaishi review – Studio Ghibli’s genius brings his concerto to a rapt London
articles.description: Royal Albert Hall, London The Royal Philharmonic rode the bucking rhythms of the star composer’s intricate score, the highlight of an evening that also included works by Steve Reich and David Lang If anyone tells you that classical music is dead you need just two words to refute them: Joe Hisaishi. The 75-year-old Japanese conductor, composer and pianist may be best known for his soundtracks, particularly his long association with Hayao Miyazaki’s Studio Ghibli films, but has parlayed his popular success into serious concert-hall credentials. You can debate style and genre, but there’s no arguing with the impact of a man who can sell out the Royal Albert Hall on a Monday night in November with an evening of music by Steve Reich, David Lang and Hisaishi himself – and not a film score in sight. Continue reading...

articles.title: First Children’s Booker prize reveals ‘Great Eight’ shortlist
articles.description: Judge Frank Cottrell-Boyce introduces the eight titles shortlisted for the inaugural £50,000 award, by authors including Shaun Tan, Eoin Colfer and Liz Hyder Books by the Oscar-winning artist Shaun Tan, Artemis Fowl author Eoin Colfer and Nero award-winner Liz Hyder are among the eight titles shortlisted for the first Children’s Booker prize. Explore the shortlist for the Children’s Booker prize 2027 and, for a limited time, get all eight books for £80 at guardianbookshop.com . Delivery charges may apply. Continue reading...

articles.title: Kate Bush and Grace Jones urge Australian government not to legalise AI ‘theft’
