articles.title: The secret to the perfect Christmas party cocktail
articles.description: Festive drinks are all about capturing the warmth and theatre of the season, so lean into wintry flavours such as orange and cloves, and add a bit of drama by bringing out the blowtorch What are the best cocktails to make for a Christmas party? Dan, by email We’re all in favour of getting the party season started early, Dan, so now is as good a time as any to get your drinks cupboard in order. “Ultimately, Christmas cocktails are all about bringing a little warmth, nostalgia and theatre, so don’t be afraid to have fun with seasonal flavours,” says Josie Pink, author of River Cottage: Cocktails and Botanicals . The smell of orange, be it fresh or dried, is never too far away at this time of year, and one reason Pink suggests having a batch of orange liquor on hand, not least “to rustle up a margarita or two”. Ditto dried citrus wheels: “They’re a must,” she says. “Not only are they gorgeous for adorning cocktails, but any misshapes can be turned into marmalade dust, and any spares into home decorations.” Pink also advises getting some syrups in your arsenal – “I’d opt for a batch of trusty vanilla syrup” – plus a chai number “for those fragrant, warming spice flavours that we all as

articles.title: Turkey gets a glowup: how a Chinese BBQ spot remade the Thanksgiving bird
articles.description: Chicago’s Sun Wah BBQ started a new Turkey Day tradition for immigrants and other neighbors: allowing them to bring in their fowl and roast it in the fragrant Hong Kong-style Tell us: do you have a special new year food tradition? Behind an Uptown Chicago facade of glass and green-glazed bricks, rows of mahogany-red ducks glisten. This neighborhood is sometimes called “New Chinatown”, sometimes “Little Vietnam ”. And this tidy restaurant is Sun Wah BBQ , which Eric and Lynda Cheng opened in 1987. Today, it’s also an unlikely Thanksgiving destination. Continue reading...

articles.title: Crunch time: Niki Segnit’s five rules for winter salads
articles.description: Plus five fantastic recipes, from seared tuna and potato to spicy butternut and lentil, to show how it’s done Approach a winter salad as you would your winter wardrobe – with clever layering. With the greatest respect to Coco Chanel, and her famous rule about taking one item off when you think you’re done, in this instance I favour assembling a salad and then adding an ingredient. Unlike in baking, where departing from a recipe can have its risks, improvisation rewards the salad maker. Still, if you’re planning a winter salad, especially if it’s a main meal, you might want to use a checklist to avoid some common pitfalls. The most egregious of these is cosy dullness. It’s all too easy to throw together some fresh winter produce and end up with a dish that’s more like a cold risotto or yesterday’s traybake. This often comes down to the combination of roasted root vegetables and “interesting” grains. What makes a salad a salad is its invigorating qualities, but root veg and cereals are sweet, with earthy, nutty flavours and soft textures; the pairing might be a modern classic but it’s about as invigorating as a warm bath. Not that you should avoid the combination; you just want to ba

articles.title: Thomasina Miers’ recipe for fried fish with red pipián, and celeriac and leek rice
articles.description: Packed with flavour and natural goodness, spicy Mexican pipián sauce goes brilliantly with white fish, while a garlicky vegetable rice is perfect on the side As the weather closes in, I find my cooking naturally moving towards comfort as well as goodness. I have been ill recently, and while my natural inclination is to cook food that I want to eat, our bodies are clever organisms and, as is often the case, the food we crave is often the food that our systems need. A pipián is rather like a revved-up Mexican korma, with toasted, ground pumpkin seeds adding a deliciously nutty backdrop to charred tomatoes, fruity, mild guajillo chillies and light spices. It is a wonderful thing to eat with fried fish on a cold night. The garlicky, celeriac-studded rice is the perfect accompaniment. Continue reading...

articles.title: Was Benjamin Franklin the original wellness bro? I lived like him for a day to find out
articles.description: Before online influencers existed, the founding father published an annual wellness pamphlet. I followed his 13 virtues he found necessary for a good life Benjamin Franklin doesn’t get enough credit. Yes, he was a founding father of the United States; he invented the lightning rod and his face is printed on $100 bills. But rarely is he celebrated for his contributions to the most meaningful field of human achievement: wellness influencing. Centuries before GRWM videos and scientifically dubious podcasts were a dollar-sign-shaped glint in their creators’ eyes, Franklin was doling out life advice. Under the pseudonym Poor Richard, Franklin published an annual pamphlet and minted maxims like “Diligence is the mother of good luck” and “Fish and visitors stink after three days.” Continue reading...

You might energise yourself ahead of your morning gym session with a few caffeinated scoops of a pre-workout supplement. articles.title: Why I love Rome in winter: ‘We reclaim the city and slip back into familiar routines’
articles.description: There is plenty of sunshine, the tourists have thinned out – and no one does a traditional Christmas like the Romans There was a time when, during a Rome winter, I would crave the warmer months. Not any more. The combination of intense heat and overtourism has made summer poco piacevole , as Italians would say – not very pleasant. So come mid-September, when the temperature drops and the crowds thin out, our mood lifts as we reclaim the city and slip back into familiar routines. In winter, the temperature is mostly mild and there is still plenty of sunshine (we do tend to grumble if the rain and grey skies persist for a few days). Rome is best seen on foot, and my favourite time to walk it is on a Sunday. Until earlier this year, I lived in Esquilino, a vibrant neighbourhood close to Termini train station. I’d begin with coffee at Gatsby Cafe by Piazza Vittorio before walking along Via Merulana – a tree-lined street similar to a Parisian boulevard – and then through the Colle Oppio park, past the Colosseum and towards Circo Massimo . Continue reading...

articles.title: The pest I’ll never forget: the cockerel whose crowing almost destroyed me
articles.description: When a neighbour installed a braying bird on the roof of our block of flats, the noise was relentless from sunrise till sunset. It became the sinister soundtrack to my life You can’t choose your family or your colleagues. And you definitely can’t choose your neighbours: the people with whom you involuntarily share a postcode and the ritual of swapping misdelivered Amazon parcels. For the most part, the neighbours in my block of flats are reassuringly neighbourly. During lockdown, I became unofficial IT support for one trying to home-school her son. I spent years emailing a PR man about Guardian celebrity interviews without realising he lived two doors away. And one of my neighbours (and now my hero) used to be in the 80s punk band Splodgenessabounds, who sang Two Pints of Lager and a Packet of Crisps Please. The other half I couldn’t pick out of a police lineup, although I certainly know their habits, from the phantom non-recycler who bungs all their plastic bottles and newspapers in the normal black bin, to the mystery resident who happily leaves the security gate open. But the one that is lodged most firmly in my memory is the neighbour who, last year, kept a pet cockerel on the

articles.title: Houseplant hacks: does grouping plants together increase humidity?
articles.description: It will help during winter months, but there are better solutions for really thirsty plants The problem With the onset of winter, the heating comes on, humidity drops and tropical plants that yearn for rainforest conditions end up in something closer to a desert. Cue crispy leaf edges. Humidifiers work, but they require buying, filling and cleaning. Misting works, but you need to remember to do it. So, a free, lazy alternative has an obvious appeal. The hack This hack is based on transpiration. Plants constantly release water vapour through their leaves, so huddling them together raises the humidity around them. Continue reading...

articles.title: Country diary: A close watch on this autumn’s leaf fall – it’s been unpredictable | Elizabeth-Jane Burnett
articles.description: Creedy Valley, Devon: Three oaks in a row – one is green, one is bronze and the other is shedding its golden leaves like a shaken snow globe Leaves fall from the oak on the brow of the hill in a flurry. There is only a slight wind, yet it is as though a snow globe has been shaken – so many leaves are animated. The process seems to take a long time. Mesmerised, I follow as they glitter to the ground. There are oaks on either side of this one. To the right, despite its close proximity, the tree has not felt the same call to let its leaves go. Instead, it holds them close – a burnished bronze, brighter even than its neighbour’s gold. To the left, a greener tree stands on the end of the line. Continue reading...

articles.title: How a tiny rare frog became an ecological warning sign for Madagascar

articles.title: Belfast Flood Alleviation Scheme Sept 14-18
articles.description: Belfast Tidal Flood Alleviation Scheme Training Exercise A training exercise to install the temporary defences will take place between 14 – 18 September 2026. There may also be some short-term disruption and temporary footpath closures at other locations. Advisory signs will be provided where necessary, including along the towpath. articles.title: NI Water Works - Cornagrade Road Enniskillen 3 Aug
articles.description: Essential Water Infrastructure Improvement Work gets underway – Cornagrade Road, Enniskillen NI Water is set to commence an upgrade of the water infrastructure on Cornagrade Road, Enniskillen in early August for approximately 6 weeks. The work will see around 400m of new watermain being laid along Cornagrade Road, starting at Cherrymount Roundabout on Monday 3 rd August and progressing as far as the second entrance to Kilmacormick Road. To facilitate the laying of this new watermain, a lane closure will be in place around each working area and signage will be in place. Working areas will be kept as short as possible (around 100m) with temporary traffic lights in place to manage the flow of traffic. Access to residential and business properties on and adjacent to Cornagrade Road will be available at all times, although parking spaces within the working area will be affected for a short period of time while the pipelaying passes. Any bus stop located within a working area will be temporarily relocated.

articles.title: Derry - NIW Scheme - Racecourse Rd - from 27 July
articles.description: Essential water network upgrade to get underway on Racecourse Road, Ballyarnett NI Water is set to begin an essential watermain upgrade on Racecourse Road, Ballyarnett (Derry/Londonderry) on Monday 27 th July to improve the resilience of the local water supply network. The work, which involves laying around 170 metres of new watermain between Carnhill Roundabout and Greenhaw Road, will replace a section of the 50-year-old Ballyarnett Water Trunkmain which has been prone to bursts. The upgrade will help to protect homes from flooding, should a burst occur in the future, and provide improved access for NI Water maintenance. A l ane closure controlled by temporary traffic lights will be in place on Racecourse Road around the working area from Monday 27 th July for four weeks. A further two weeks of work will take place in the adjacent verge which will not require any traffic management. Temporary traffic lights will be manned during peak hours and access to properties will be maintained at all times, although parking spaces within the working area will be temporarily unavailable. Once the lane closure is removed, works will move into the adjacent verge to complete the final phase of w

articles.title: Craigavon - Closure of Maple Path & Parkmore Footbridges
articles.description: Closure of Maple Path and Parkmore Footbridges, Craigavon The Department for Infrastructure have announced that the Maple Path and Parkmore footbridges in Craigavon will be closed from Thursday 4 June 2026. Detailed engineering inspections identified structural concerns, and it has been concluded that the closure of these footbridges is necessary while a permanent solution is developed. Alternative local walking routes are available and will be signposted where appropriate. While these routes may increase journey times for some users, they will provide access around the affected areas. The Department recognises the importance of both footbridges to local residents and apologises for any inconvenience caused. However, as the Department’s infrastructure assets age there will always be an eventual need to replace structures that present safety issues or have come to the end of their natural lifespan. Further information on future proposals for the bridges will be provided as work progresses. The Department would like to thank the public for their patience and cooperation.

articles.title: Congo Halts Cobalt Exports As Price Collapse Fuels Resource Nationalism
articles.description: Congo Halts Cobalt Exports As Price Collapse Fuels Resource Nationalism The Democratic Republic of Congo is using its dominance in cobalt production to restrict exports in an interventionist move to reverse the collapse in global prices. Bloomberg reports that ARECOMS, the country's strategic minerals regulator, has imposed a ban on cobalt exports that will take effect at the end of November to combat plunging prices for the metal, which is widely used in EV batteries. ARECOMS said the decision is intended " to address the oversupply in the international market and to promote a sustainable rebalancing of the market ." The decision marks Congo's second export ban since February 2025 ( read here ), and it  exemplifies the use of resource nationalism to influence global cobalt prices . This theme is becoming all too familiar and is growing worldwide.  The first suspension lasted eight months before being replaced by quotas that restricted shipments to less than half the country's 2024 output. The LME cobalt cash price has plunged by about 40%, from around $55,000 per metric ton in late summer to roughly $33,000 in recent weeks. Cobalt is primarily used in lithium-ion batteries for EVs

articles.description: The Real Reason Trump Wanted Jensen Back? Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia was a market rescue before it was a national security call , if Fox Business' Charles Gasparino has it right. His sources say that after last week's AI-stock rout, major investors told people close to the White House the probability was "near 100%" that the country was heading for a recession, because the unwinding AI trade would hit spending "across the tech ecosystem." That warning, Gasparino reports, is "seen as the major reason" Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent "suddenly joined his boss" in calling for Huang's reinstatement, "because it would at least temporarily pause the market convulsion." Eight days ago Bessent told Nvidia's board to look outside the company for Huang's successor. By Sunday he was calling the spy angle "kind of a canard." articles.description: Montana Judge Blocks State's Law Defining Biological Sex Authored by Savannah Hulsey Pointer via The Epoch Times , Montana has been blocked from enforcing a law that would define sex as based on a person's reproductive system. Missoula County District Court Judge Leslie Halligan granted a preliminary injunction on Nov. 16 in a lawsuit brought on behalf of a group of Montanans, including transgender and intersex plaintiffs. The judge's order regards Senate Bill 437, which established definitions for the terms "male," "female," "sex," and "gender" as applied to Montana law. The legislation defines sex according to biological features, including reproductive organs. It also treats gender as synonymous with sex, instead of allowing for reliance on gender identity. The injunction prevents the state from enforcing those definitions until the case is resolved, but it does not strike down the law. Halligan was of the opinion that the plaintiffs are likely to succeed in their case, arguing that the law violated Montana's constitutional protections for both privacy and equal treatment. articles.title: Don't Even Boil It: California City Warns Residents Not To Drink Tap Water After Suspicious Tank 'Tampering' Alarm
articles.description: Don't Even Boil It: California City Warns Residents Not To Drink Tap Water After Suspicious Tank 'Tampering' Alarm The City of San Luis Obispo told residents of its Serrano and Patricia neighborhoods early Monday not to drink or cook with their tap water, after an intrusion alarm at a city drinking water storage tank indicated trespassing and possible tampering. The city's "Do Not Drink" notice went out at about 3:30 a.m. Officials said the break-in raised concerns that an unknown substance may have been introduced into the drinking water. The alarm tripped on Sunday evening, Nov. 22, according to KEYT . Crews drained the tank and flushed the water lines around it. The city has not said whether anyone actually got into the water, or whether anything was put in it. Residents in the affected area were told to use bottled water for drinking, baby formula, juice, brushing teeth, washing dishes, making ice and cooking. The city also warned them not to boil, filter or otherwise treat the tap water , since none of that would make it safe if something had been added. "Keep using bottled water until the city confirms that testing shows the tap water is safe to drink," the city said Monday.

articles.title: Keepsake County review – eccentric stealing simulator with a social conscience
articles.description: PC; Forward Instinct This irreverent stealth game depicts Samuel’s lonely life robbing garish, midwestern abodes – it’s a Shameless way to make a living For many people, McMansions are an eyesore, but for the protagonist of Keepsake County, a renowned burglar, they are an enticing opportunity. Prowling at purple-hued dusk, this unfussy thief is just as likely to steal a half-eaten slice of pizza or a naff ceramic ornament as he is an expensive set of golf clubs. It’s a sad, desperate way to make a living, a sense compounded by what this fledgling kleptomaniac carries his loot away in: a plastic shopping bag. Countless works have taken us to breadline America, from classic novel East of Eden to acclaimed TV crime drama Mare of Easttown. But Keepsake County is no prestige examination of the economic underbelly of the US. Rather, it is a stealing simulator with eccentric Adult Swim-style art and a darkly absurdist sense of humour that is expressed in its moment-to-moment action. For example, when I set off the alarm at a glinting modernist abode, I had to quickly dodge the gunshot fired my way by its maniacal owner, and as I scarpered across the surrounding grassy verge, I grabbed und

articles.title: ‘The place becomes a jewellery box of glittering lights’: readers’ favourite winter city breaks in Europe
articles.description: Ice-skating, illuminated medieval buildings and seasonal treats feature in your picks of atmospheric winter cities • Tell us about a winter weekend break – the best tip wins a £200 holiday voucher In December, Antwerp is transformed into a jewellery box of glittering lights. Christmas markets throng the historic squares, and the illuminated facades of the gothic and Renaissance buildings create a magical atmosphere. At Groenplaats, we watched ice-skaters circle the statue of Rubens, while at Handschoenmarkt we listened to carols courtesy of the Singing Christmas Tree. There’s plenty to do during the daytime, too: we admired the art nouveau architecture in Zurenborg and paid homage to Bruegel’s Dull Gret at Museum Mayer van den Bergh . The famous brown cafes make the perfect place for a cosy nightcap. Emily Continue reading...

articles.title: Eat your cup: could edible packaging help solve the world’s plastic problem?
articles.description: Experts say seaweed could be a solution in the fight against global plastic waste, which doubled between 2000 and 2019 The name of the Northamptonshire hamlet of Nobottle means “new building” in Old English. But on a Tuesday last month, the name of the tiny cluster of houses in the East Midlands took on a whole different meaning. Parked on a driveway opposite the village green, a van handed out Innocent ginger shots with one notable difference: there was no bottle. The drinks were in edible pods as part of a pilot project with Notpla, a company that makes biodegradable packaging. Roughly half of the 30 or so local residents tried the product lined up on trays. Continue reading...

articles.title: Measles is officially back in the USA. Will Maha pay the price? - video
articles.description: This week the US lost its measles elimination status, an official recognition that the infectious disease is endemic in the country after being eliminated for 26 years. To find out what this means in practical terms for citizens, Ian Sample hears from the Guardian US health reporter Jessica Glenza. She explains why it comes at an already difficult time for the health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, and his Make America Healthy Again movement, and what newly elected Democrats will be focusing on when it comes to health Continue reading...

articles.title: Consent under scrutiny: where does youth end and adulthood begin?
articles.description: After the Brand and Walliams revelations, calls for a ‘staggered’ age of consent are redefining what makes someone ‘adult’ The fact that the age of sexual consent in Britain is set at 16 is thanks to a chimney sweep’s daughter from Marylebone, London, called Eliza Armstrong – not that she had any say in the matter. In June 1885, Armstrong had just turned 13 when she was sold for sex by her alcoholic mother for the sum of £5. She believed she was going to work as a gentleman’s maid; instead, the child was taken to a brothel, where she was examined to prove she was a virgin and drugged with chloroform to await the gentleman who had “purchased” her virginity. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Guide #270: Grand Theft Auto VI is everywhere – but is it really the cultural event of the decade?
articles.description: In this week’s newsletter: It could be the biggest entertainment release ever, but its reach reveals the limit of shared cultural experience An estimated cost of $1bn. A development period of 13 years. A production team of 5,000 people. A game map the size of Manchester. An estimated 24m copies sold through pre-orders and launch day alone, generating $2.36bn. Thousands upon thousands of days of leave booked and sick days taken to play the thing, costing the US economy an estimated $1bn (yep, another billion figure) in lost productivity. The scale of Grand Theft Auto VI – and the tidal wave of facts and figures surrounding its making and economic impact – truly boggles the mind. Even if you, like me, are unlikely to ever sit down and play the thing, you will struggle to escape its influence. Footage both sinister and benign – from graphic shooting sprees to mellow clips of its protagonists strolling, hand in hand, down the beach – will follow you around Facebook, Instagram, X and TikTok. Whatever your preferred publication, left or right, high- or lowbrow, it will have proffered its own take on the game, whether it’s to bemoan its godless influence on adolescent men or to laud its u

articles.title: Why I love Stockholm in winter: ‘A return to slowing down, cosying up and revering every glimmer of light’
articles.description: Swedes adore the festive season, embracing the shorter days with fairy lights, yuletide feasts and fun in the snow I’ll let you in on a secret: I often tell people that summer is the best time to visit Stockholm. Clouds drift across impossibly blue skies, we skip around midsummer maypoles singing folk songs and cruise the waterways, bobbing and weaving through the archipelago’s 30,000-plus islands. That’s mostly because I want to keep December in Stockholm to myself. Soft white snow dusts buildings of ochre and burnt sienna like icing on a cake. Festive candles light up pavements leading to cosy cafes, where the earthy, buttery smell of seasonal saffron buns ( lussekatter ) replaces cinnamon buns for fika , our revered tradition of coffee and cake. Continue reading...

articles.title: Hacks, AI and conspiracy theories: why are we having so many outages?
articles.description: After chaos at airlines, banks and companies from Microsoft to Apple, people have become convinced the world’s systems are under attack Nicole Reindorf’s American Airlines flight was ready for takeoff in Phoenix when the pilot came on the intercom and announced what was to become the longest nationwide aviation shutdown since 9/11 . Reindorf, 70, had seen the headlines hours before about a global Microsoft outage . She immediately suspected the two were linked in some way by AI-related threats – and that she would not get to the wedding of her best friend’s son in California. Continue reading...

articles.title: Cassette, London WC2: ‘One of the greatest dishes I’ve eaten all year’ – restaurant review | Grace Dent on restaurants
articles.description: A discombobulating brew of the seemingly casual with the deadly bloody serious I booked my lunch table at Cassette , a new French restaurant in Covent Garden, central London, while watching a viral video of a blasé Parisian couple , mid-riot, sipping wine and smoking Gauloises near the Arc de Triomphe. Yes, fiery flames of mass anarchy, but also, yes, finishing one’s glass is important, too. The Brits keep opening Parisian-style restaurants as a quiet admission that these people are really bloody cool, and this new one from Mark Gurney and Matt Bushnell , the pair behind Peckham’s Levan (also very cool, incidentally), serves the likes of a coq au vin jaune pie with a chicken leg saluting from its crust, and panisse with chopped mussels and green tomato. There’s also pork chop with sauce Talleyrand, Maldon oysters with beurre blanc, and a cocktail called Jet Fuel that combines Get 27 , the green mint liqueur that gives every Parisian a starry-eyed memory of their parents’ dinner parties, with calvados and coffee liqueur. Cassette is a discombobulating brew of the seemingly casual with the actually deadly bloody serious. Yes, dress up fancy, if you wish, but you can also slide in her

articles.title: The footballer-turned-BookTuber who made an obscure Tolstoy novella a belated bestseller
articles.description: Once named the best player in Brazil, Gustavo Scarpa’s literature obsession has inspired thousands to become bookworms Julián Scatolaro noticed something odd was occurring when several people came into his bookshop over the space of a few days, all asking for Leo Tolstoy’s novella The Death of Ivan Ilyich . The 35-year-old, who owns a bookshop in the small Argentine city of Chajarí, 311 miles from Buenos Aires, said the sudden interest in a book written in 1886 was surprising enough. But this was particularly strange because when his customers ask for works by the Russian writer, they usually want War and Peace . In a video he posted about the mystery, he called it the “ Tolstoy enigma ”. Continue reading...

articles.title: How can we explain psychosomatic illnesses?
articles.description: Emotions play a significant part in physical symptoms – but not in the way people often imagine When Diego started seeing bright flashing lights in his field of vision and felt his legs go weak, he thought he knew immediately what was happening. His mother had a stroke in her 60s, and although Diego was active and (unlike his mother) didn’t smoke, he had always expected that the same would happen to him. So it was a huge relief to be told – after seeing a stroke specialist and having a brain scan – that he had not had a stroke at all. Unfortunately the relief was short-lived. The visual disturbances and the weakness were real and debilitating. If this wasn’t a stroke, what was it? Some illnesses aren’t caused by disease or damage, but arise when the coordinated functioning of the body goes awry. In a percentage of these cases a person’s psychological health is an important element in their symptoms. Intuitively this seems mysterious. We are accustomed to thinking about physical symptoms as being caused by physical events; viruses, inflammation, bleeding. How can something as intangible as a thought have any impact on something as physical as a leg? How can the mind make us ill? Con

articles.title: How to make nasi goreng – recipe | Felicity Cloake's Masterclass
articles.description: The richly flavoured Indonesian and Malaysian fried-rice dish is quick to cook, but calls for a little groundwork. Here’s how to make it Unless you’ve had the admirable foresight to prepare the spice paste in advance, thus turning this into just a quick assembly job, nasi goreng is not a fried rice that you whip up in five minutes from last night’s leftovers. Neither, however, is it particularly complex, and the richly savoury, shallot-sweet base gives it a depth of flavour that more than justifies the modest investment of time. Prep 25 min Chill 2 hr+ Cook 5 min Serves 2 Continue reading...

articles.title: Nine Night is back and proves itself a modern classic full of secrets, squabbles and laughs
articles.description: Kiln theatre, London Exquisitely acted, and directed with lightness and depth, Natasha Gordon’s 2018 tragicomedy about a Jamaican matriarch’s wake is moving and never mawkish The death of a parent has a way of blowing up the lives of family members it leaves behind. The combustions of grief, greed and secrets revealed around a barely buried coffin litter the tragicomic works of playwrights such as Tracy Letts (August: Osage County) and Branden Jacobs-Jenkins (Appropriate). You might want to add Natasha Gordon’s debut play to that canon, although it comes wrapped in its own distinct cultural tradition. Its structure revolves around the Caribbean funeral ritual that commemorates the death of a loved one over nine nights. A debut play written by a young Black British woman, featuring an almost entirely Black British cast, it got a huge reaction at the National Theatre in 2018 . Continue reading...

articles.title: Sounds may seem louder or even painful as you age. Here’s why
articles.description: For some, everyday loud noise becomes bothersome. Researchers call this sound hypersensitivity and it’s worth knowing whether it’s due to ageing or not Loud noises bother some people more as they get older – the clatter of plates or shrieking children, which once blended into the background, now seem utterly intolerable. If that’s you, it’s worth knowing what’s due to normal ageing and what isn’t. Continue reading...

articles.title: Cat’s whiskers: Nan Goldin proves that she’s the greatest US artist since Warhol – review
articles.description: Hayward Gallery, London The photographer finds echoes of Caravaggio and Greek myth in her erotic images, while her disturbing animal montages show that while humans can be beautiful, we are far from innocent It’s the dirty realism of Nan Goldin ’s images, her unfazed photography of the rough seams of spontaneous, dangerous lives, that enables her to create a film of such unlikely ambition as Stendhal Syndrome. This ecstatic condition is named after the French novelist who in 1817 fell ill in Florence, after gorging on the beauty of the Renaissance city’s treasures until “I had palpitations of the heart … I walked with the fear of falling”. Goldin, too, has suffered a bout of this aesthetic delirium, not in Italy but Paris – “the first time I was alone in the Louvre”, she explains on screen. She infects you with it in a ravishing work housed in what looks like a bronze yurt entered via a vaulted corridor. If this seems ostentatious, the film justifies the ceremony. A montage of sensual images teems with Goldin’s uniquely raw, immediate feel for the human presence as she photographs her friends, mostly in the nude, legs wrapped round each other, or lying in a swoon, or touching thems

The Duo sits atop the pile as Apple’s most expensive smartphone – at £1,999 (€2,299/$1,999/A$3,499) it costs more than most of its folding Android rivals and as much as the iPhone 18 Pro Max and the latest iPad mini combined. articles.title: A taste of Italy: Alessandro Giannatempo’s recipes for Amalfi-style ricotta and pear cake, and crocodile’s porridge
articles.description: Sweet from top to toe: a creamy, southern Italian fruit and nut cake, and an almondy polenta porridge from the north Although I grew up in Emilia-Romagna, my family history spans the Italian peninsula. Inspired by my mixed upbringing, these recipes reflect the flavours of both southern and northern Italy. The Amalfi-style ricotta and pear cake, as the name suggests, is a nod to the southern coast of Salerno. Fresh ricotta is whipped with lemony pears and sandwiched between layers of nutty hazelnut cake. The crocodile’s porridge, named after a traditional Italian beverage made with milk and pear juice, combines northern ingredients such as polenta and amaro for a very cosy stovetop-made dessert – or breakfast, if you ask me! Continue reading...

articles.title: Country diary: Top deck of the bus for the finest views of autumn | John Gilbey
articles.description: Gwynedd: Past golden hillsides and the great Cadair Idris, through wooded valleys, to the starting point for my walk The morning starts bright but cold, with a hazy mist clinging to the trees across the valley. This could be one of the last good weather days, so I take the bus north into Gwynedd, clambering awkwardly upstairs to get the best view of the autumn colours. The mist begins to clear and, in a wet meadow, a heron stands alertly by a ditch, watching for movement. Beyond the Afon Dyfi, the hills are golden with patches of larch and the deeper orange tones of the oak and ash. Well-defined shadows below the dark blue sky shelter pockets of still-frosted gloom, as we cross the Dyfi into Gwynedd. Continue reading...

articles.title: How freaked out should we be? After mass outages, experts tell us how close we are to ‘doomsday’
articles.description: As tech, travel and banking failures sweep the US, analysts and cyber-security directors discuss AI, underfunding and what keeps them up at night Grounded flights. Bank websites crashing. Microsoft Outlook outages grinding business operations to a halt. Zoom, Ikea, and PokerStars websites hacked. In the past weeks, there’s been a distinct sense that the complex systems that undergird our daily life might be on the verge of total collapse. Or, at the very least, they seem pretty wobbly. Even those who aren’t prone to conspiracy theories have been wondering out loud if these recent disruptions are somehow connected. Speculation runs wild about targeted cyber-attacks by Iranian hackers, or AI agents autonomously hacking critical (air traffic, banking) and not-so-critical (the Ikea website) infrastructure. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘One area of the tent was known as fart corner’: what it’s really like to be on The Great British Bake Off
articles.description: As we come to the end of another series, former contestants including Kim-Joy, Syabira Yusoff and Christiaan de Vries reminisce on their time in the tent – and the aftermath The Great British Bake Off is just about to finish its best season in years. Like a cloud of Swiss meringue buttercream on a slightly sunken cake, Nigella Lawson has added glamour and indulgence to a format that needed saving. But this year’s contestants have brought the joy, too: talented, charismatic individuals who have interrupted their lives to spend three months with bits of dough stuck to their elbows and indigestion from all the recipe testing. We spoke to five previous contestants to find out why they put themselves through it, and what they feel they achieved in the process. The scale runs from “a very nice level of X-list celebrity” to “a better version of me”, with a lot of life lessons (and a fart corner) along the way. Continue reading...

He was wounded twice and twice sent back to the front. On 11 May 2025, after 20 months at war, he was killed in the village of Uspenovka, near the eastern Ukrainian city of Pokrovsk, aged 52. articles.description: The Summer I Turned Pretty’s Christopher Briney and 1923’s Michelle Randolph try their best, but this chaotic cross-country journey is not worth taking Credit where credit is due: it takes some nerve for Amazon to open its latest holiday romcom, Clashing Through the Snow, with characters bemoaning the enervated state of the book industry. Publishing isn’t the cultural epicenter it once was, reports boutique press head Jeremy (PJ Byrne) before announcing some impending new year’s layoffs. Alas, things have changed – “if Faulkner were alive today, he’d be making ASMR videos with Mr Beast” (or, perhaps, competing on Prime Video’s Beast Games?) Self-awareness can be key to the ludicrous joys of a Christmas romcom confection, though Clashing Through the Snow, starring 1923’s Michelle Randolph and homegrown Amazon star Christopher Briney (The Summer I Turned Pretty), tests one’s patience for beating you to the branded punchline. Briney’s Ryan, a numbers-driven, macro-counting kind of book editor, pitches a “financial trends with benefits” romance that could be “Rebecca Yarros big”. Soulmates, says Randolph’s rival workhorse editor Hannah, are as mythical as “ethical billionaires and pain

articles.description: The longest ever Cop climate talks have ended in failure after countries were unable to agree a deal. The key sticking point was the omission of any mention of fossil fuels in the final draft. To find out how it all went so wrong and what could come next, Madeleine Finlay speaks to Guardian environment editor Fiona Harvey who has been in Antalya, Turkey covering the talks. Continue reading...

articles.title: Words are not enough after the Myanmar genocide ruling. The world can do better – but it must take these steps | Gordon Brown
articles.description: Atrocities happen again and again. We need a comprehensive framework that would allow us to predict, prevent or respond to them For the first time a state, Myanmar, has been found directly responsible for the crime of genocide . On the instructions of the country’s Tatmadaw regime, at least 10,000 Rohingya men, women and children were murdered, and thousands more were subjected to sexual violence and torture in a 2017 military campaign. While the international court of justice ruled a decade after the crimes that they amounted to genocide, it is unclear whether Myanmar’s leaders will ever be brought to justice, whether any of the more than 1 million Rohingya refugees will be able to return home or whether the country’s government will even have to pay reparations for its crimes. Gordon Brown was UK prime minister from 2007 to 2010 Continue reading...

articles.title: You Can See Everything tells us nothing about Elizabeth Holmes. I guess that’s what the courts are for | Zoe Williams
articles.description: The Theranos founder talks in frustrating riddles – but was she lying to us, or to herself? Or could she be a cog in a larger, more sinister, lie-machine? I went to see You Can See Everything with a friend who had never heard of Elizabeth Holmes, the disgraced founder of blood testing startup Theranos. She knew that she was a convicted fraudster, because as the film opens, Holmes is 34 days from commencing her prison sentence for defrauding investors. But she was completely open-minded as to whether this was definitely fraud or a miscarriage of justice, whether Holmes was the puppeteer or the puppet (of her previous business and romantic partner, Sunny Balwani, who was also convicted of fraud), and whether Holmes’s central claim, of huge diagnostic capabilities from putting a drop of blood into a tiny box, had any scientific foundation. My friend was probably the co-director Nathan Fielder’s perfect viewer, someone who had no preconceptions about what was true: what would she learn, from three hours with a camera so close to the subject’s face that you could count her eyelashes? “Well … She seems nice?” she said after the film had finished. I veer towards the old-fashioned and deep

articles.title: Kemi is beside herself that Burnham is trying to salvage a Brexit deal. Can’t we all stop talking about it? | John Crace
articles.description: Badenoch ends her anti-EU speech by calling herself ‘the leader of common sense’. Really? When you’ve got David Cameron, Theresa May, Boris Johnson and Rishi Sunak saying you’ve got it wrong on Brexit , then the chances are Andy Burnham must be doing something right. These four are the former prime ministers that are largely responsible for the mess the UK is currently in. Lord Big Dave had never really given the possibility of leaving the EU much thought. The Maybot spent three years saying nothing more intelligent than “Brexit means Brexit”. Boris lied through his teeth to get his deal over the line. And as for Rishi? It’s hard to think of anything he achieved. All of which makes life tricky for Kemi Badenoch. Because in an ideal world, Kemi would rather we all forgot about Brexit entirely. Not because it is going so well, but because it it isn’t. She would like you to believe that Brexit was nothing to do with her – even though she was a hardline Brexiter – or the Tories. Rather it was some kind of paranormal event that just happened to the country while the Conservatives were in power. Correlation does not imply causality and all that. In KemiWorld we would pretend that everyth

articles.title: The ruling against Myanmar makes proving genocide more feasible | Kenneth Roth
articles.description: The international court of justice has settled questions over the issue of intent, with powerful implications for Israel The international court of justice (ICJ) decision last Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya recognizes the plight of one of the world’s most persecuted minorities. It also resonates in Gaza, where the same court is now more likely to find that Israel committed genocide against Palestinians. That possibility has incensed the Donald Trump administration, but it should think twice before attacking another international tribunal. Continue reading...

articles.description: The manager’s first game in charge was a disaster and he needs to lift the mood within a sunken squad if a relegation battle is to be avoided Sign up for our free newsletter here In as much as any derby can ever be a free hit, there was always a sense that Mauricio Pochettino’s first game as Manchester United manager wouldn’t matter too much; nobody expected them to win away to Liverpool. This was not a game on which anybody was going to judge him, and that feeling only magnified when Leny Yoro was sent off after eight minutes. United’s victory at Anfield last season was their first for a decade; what’s difficult to do with 11 men is only going to get harder playing a man down for 82 minutes. But that does not mean that it did not matter. Although Roy Keane was determined to reject the suggestion, there was perhaps even some credit to be gleaned from having lost only 4-0 . Certainly when they were 2-0 down after 13 minutes, there was reason for United to fear an embarrassment akin to their 7-0 defeat against Liverpool in 2023 . Perhaps Pochettino deserves credit for his switch to a back three, which brought a degree of stabilisation, but United could easily have lost far more comfo

articles.title: Nations Championship finals weekend to kick off in front of 40,000 empty seats
articles.description: Organisers to close top tier of Allianz Stadium on Friday Saturday and Sunday sales stronger with 70% taken The opening night of the inaugural Nations Championship finals weekend on Friday is poised to be played in front of around 40,000 empty seats, with the top tier of the Allianz Stadium in Twickenham to be closed. The Guardian has learned that more than 50% of tickets at the 82,000-capacity venue for the Ireland v Australia/Italy v Fiji double-header remained available on Monday. That figure could grow after tournament organisers opened a ticket swap exchange for fans wanting to watch their team. Continue reading...

articles.title: Game over? How playing Grand Theft Auto VI is affecting elite athletes’ performances | Sean Ingle
articles.description: Burning the midnight oil playing video games is not ideal preparation for professional sport – but it’s not all bad “They miss games, the cheque’s still clearing. And you’re trying to tell me they got this kind of addiction to a video game that they sitting there with their thumbs looking like Donald Trump?” That was ESPN’s Stephen A Smith, one of the US’s most provocative and influential sports pundits, spitting fire and fury last week after hearing that so many NBA and NFL stars were absorbed in Grand Theft Auto VI. Smith was hardly an outlier. Other pundits, as well as some Manchester United fans, also questioned Bryan Mbeumo’s focus and professionalism after he posted an image of GTA VI and the word “ historique ” after midnight on Thursday. Meanwhile before last weekend’s Premier League games, the Odd Sport social media account predicted that Chelsea, Brighton and Manchester City would all lose. Why? articles.description: Management team were in line for huge payouts Fifa denies Infantino would have profited from plan Gianni Infantino’s failed Fifa Forward Enterprise plan could have locked football in for up to 96 years while paying its management up to 5% of the scheme’s multibillion-pound value, according to documents seen by the Guardian. Previously undisclosed communications by Fifa and Thrive Capital, the lead investor for the proposal, cast fresh light on the deal to sell off football’s crown jewels. articles.title: Dylan Moran goes looking for trouble and disappears off the beaten track in this baffling comedy show
articles.description: Royal & Derngate, Northampton The Black Books star gets off to a promising start as he contemplates ‘the burning ball of what you don’t understand’ but his search for levity leads to half-baked ditties Is Dylan Moran joking when he opens his show by telling Northampton’s audience “I didn’t write anything, or prepare”? By the end, you wouldn’t bet on it. Bleary directionlessness may be par for the course for the Irish comic, whose work has always combined poetic-philosophical dazzle with a certain wooziness. But after a promising start tonight, his new touring show, Looking for Trouble, conspicuously loses its way, as Moran frets about forgetting a significant chunk of material, before abandoning his encore and leaving a bewildered audience in his wake. That’s a shame, because there are shards of trademark brilliance in the opening 20 minutes, which see the 55-year-old address himself, albeit obliquely, to the mysteries of being human in 2026, AKA “the burning ball of what you don’t understand” From Trump to AI, Moran surveys it all in wide angle not closeup, as symptoms of our confusion, atavism and fear of expulsion from the tribe. The quality of his thinking in this section, whil

articles.title: Chemicals, Covid and cabbage: why 2026 has been an amazing year for documentaries
articles.description: With Musk, NAZA and You Can See Everything finding large audiences, non-fiction cinema is poised to break through. But there are plenty more gripping stories waiting for their turn in the spotlight There comes a time in the life of every film enthusiast when they must set aside foolish fictions and face up to some hard truths. Specifically, that time arrives each November in the form of the International Documentary Film Festival Amsterdam (IDFA for short), with its tales of crisis and strife, angry resistance and everyday human kindness. The world’s largest documentary festival plays out in the city’s twinkling downtown district, quite near the torture museum, and provides a sharp corrective to the confected dramas and A-list pageantry of Cannes, Toronto and Venice. The forecast is bracing, stormy, and occasionally chilling. Hours of darkness; no stars. We might not wish to live in the world IDFA shows us, but unfortunately we do, and so it pays to stay informed, be engaged. This year’s lineup of 250-plus documentaries steers us around the geopolitical hot spots, from tales of forced displacement in the West Bank to the rolling hell of Gaza; from a jungle-based guerrilla army in M

articles.title: ‘Reminds me of home’: why Coming to America is my feelgood movie
articles.description: The latest in our series of writers picking their most rewatched comfort films is an ode to Eddie Murphy’s beloved culture-clash comedy “Good morning, my neighbors!” A young Eddie Murphy shouts from the balcony of a shady apartment building. In the bustling Queens neighborhood, he sticks out like a sore thumb with his foreign accent, tailored blazing jacket and red tie. “Hey, fuck you!” A voice yells from below and Murphy repeats the phrase, believing that it’s a greeting rather than an insult. It’s one of the standout scenes from the film Coming to America, because it’s so absurd but effective in that there is a cultural clash going on here. In Coming to America, Prince Akeem, played by Eddie Murphy, is the sole heir to the throne of Zamunda, a fictitious African country. Instead of having an arranged marriage, Prince Akeem exercises his autonomy and intends to find his own bride somewhere far away from the continent, much to his parents’ chagrin. With the coin-flip and a roll of the personal globe, Akeem and his sidekick Semmi go to America but more specifically Queens because where else would be more fitting to find his bride? While trying to assimilate to the fast pace of New Y

articles.title: Who Is Still Alive review – grief-stricken stories of the places and people lost in Gaza
articles.description: Nicolas Wadimoff invites refugees to draw a floor plan of their former neighbourhood, bringing raw and agonising pain to the surface A sombre documentary from the Swiss musician and film-maker Nicolas Wadimoff, who returns to his longstanding interest in Gaza. In this film, a group of survivor-refugees who made it out of Gaza and into Egypt during the bombing gather in an enclosed studio and are invited to draw out a kind of floor plan of what they remember of their neighbourhood. First, this is on paper and then on the studio floor itself; they use that as a basis for their memories of what and who they have lost. (The people who have died are described as having been “martyred”.) The result is almost unbearably painful. The raw and agonising grief, which perhaps stays just at the waterline of consciousness most of the time, is here brought above the surface. They are people suffering from trauma, carrying videos on their phones of their lost loved ones. One interviewee talks of attending the Edward Said conservatory , now rubble; another talks of her work in film-making and animation. Another man plays poignantly beautiful music on his qanun, a type of zither, and then specifies

articles.title: More sex, different endings: how fan fiction makes our dreams come true
articles.description: From Heated Rivalry to Harry Potter, popular series are inspiring fan fiction read by thousands online. Now the authors of those online works are getting publishing deals of their own Shortly after this year’s London book fair , rumours began to circulate of a seven-figure book deal for the author of the wildly popular work of Harry Potter fan fiction All the Young Dudes. First published between 2017 and 2018 by user MsKingBean89 on the online platform Archive of Our Own, All the Young Dudes is arguably the most-read work of fan fiction of all time. Now its author will write a trilogy under the pen name BN King, with the first novel, Wolfboy, due to be published in autumn 2027. This is by no means the first example of fan fiction crossing over into mainstream publishing: the bestselling debut of 2025, Alchemised, also started off as fan fiction based on the Harry Potter series, with some inspiration from The Handmaid’s Tale too. And nearly 15 years earlier, EL James published Fifty Shades of Grey, which began life as Twilight fan fiction before proceeding, in its new guise, to sell millions of copies worldwide. Continue reading...

articles.title: Bill Wyman’s Rock & Roll Lists review – greatest hits and biggest misses
articles.description: The rock critic’s obsessive yet incisive sorting of musical genius is a contrarian delight As veteran US music journalist Bill Wyman (no relation to the Stones bassist) would be the first to point out, the listicle is not a revered form of internet journalism. It labours under a ghastly portmanteau name that simply jams together “list” and “article” but somehow carries a hint of the diminutive about it, which the listicle’s detractors would say is absolutely right: a chart – a Top 20 or 50 or 100 – with each entry warranting a brief paragraph of explication, they are reviled as a cheap, largely effortless way to fill space online. They are also astoundingly popular, particularly when the subject is music, perhaps because people were compiling rock and pop’s history into listicles decades before the internet came along. The NME got there first, in 1974, with what it called a “Writers’ All-Time Top 100 Albums” list – a bold early attempt to define a canon of classic rock, with Sgt Pepper at No 1 and black and female artists sorely under­represented. But it wasn’t until the 90s that the idea really grew legs. Suddenly the music press was awash with retrospective charts, evidence that

articles.title: Adder Stone by Clare Clark review – the story of a drowned Welsh village
articles.description: A real-life flooding becomes a flashpoint in this novel exploring family relationships, female liberation and the drive for Welsh independence In the author’s note accompanying her eighth novel, Adder Stone, Clare Clark recalls first learning how a lake in the Welsh valleys shrank during the drought of 1976 only to reveal an abandoned village underneath. As a child, Clark became obsessed with the idea, envisaging a sort of Welsh Pompeii – houses and lives frozen in time, buried beneath the water and the mud. Fifty years since that uncanny occurrence, Clark’s richly researched novel seeks to tell the story of that forgotten Welsh village: not abandoned by choice, but forcibly evicted in order to make way for a new reservoir needed to service Liverpool’s growing population. Clark charts how this event had a profound impact on individual lives, but also how it served as a flashpoint in the broader conversation around Welsh independence. Continue reading...

articles.title: John M MacKenzie obituary
articles.description: Historian who transformed the understanding of empire and its role in shaping modern societies How does ruling the world change the rulers themselves? If such a question has become self-evident today, it was not the case in 1984, when John M MacKenzie, who has died aged 82, published Propaganda and Empire: The Manipulation of British Public Opinion, 1880-1960. Through his analysis of a wide range of cultural artefacts, until then neglected by historians, he articulated some of the key questions that would structure the “imperial turn”. With subsequent publications, and through Studies in Imperialism published by Manchester University Press – a book series that he launched, and edited during three decades, with more than 200 titles now published – he shifted the historical understanding of empire, treating it not as a peripheral aspect of national history, but as a central organising framework for understanding the formation of modern societies, identities, institutions and systems of power. Continue reading...

articles.title: I’ve been covering Black Friday deals for seven years – here are the rules that stop me from overspending
articles.description: Arm yourself with a list, learn how to spot a genuinely good deal and don’t give in to Fomo to shop smarter this season • Expert tips for buying refurbished phones and laptops this Black Friday I’ve been writing about Black Friday deals since 2019, and while you may think spending hours scrolling online retailers’ deals would turn me into a shopping addict, it has (fortunately) done the opposite. Retailers know that, for many of us, this is the time of year we finally buy that hefty investment we’ve been debating, or else blitz through the kids’ letter to Santa. If you play your cards right, it’s an excellent way to save cash. I’d like to think I’ve got my shopping strategy down to a fine art, so here’s how I make Black Friday work for me. Make sure you go in with the right mindset. Relentless discounts and non-stop advertising are designed to make you feel frenzied. When I panic that something will sell out and feel myself rushing to buy it, I find it helpful to close my browser, take a breather, and remember that retailers need my custom more than I need that new coat. articles.title: The one change that worked: At 21, I was terrified of seeming ‘cringe’. Then I rediscovered my inner child

articles.title: Lucy Worsley’s Keys to the Castle review – heavenly TV that instantly brightens up your day
articles.description: The brilliant historian has a gift for cheering everybody up. In this series, she discovers the delights of European castles – and makes you want to spontaneously book a holiday When I think of Lucy Worsley, I am immediately cheered up. Partly it’s the coats. (So neat! So bright! So wonder where she gets them and if I could carry one off!) Partly it’s the hairclips. (How big has she gone this time? Is it going to stay in?) But mostly it is her; her energy, her indefatigability, her determination to impart what she knows in the most accessible way and, above all, her abundant confidence without ego. It’s the latter that allows for that rare thing – other historians to be interviewed and share their knowledge with the lay person at home without the presenter champing at the bit to show that he or she knows this already and that they are just letting them simplify things for the good of the show. This is my personal bugbear, so thank you for letting me exorcise it here, and thank you to Worsley for not adding to my burdens. To feel cheerful as you approach a history lesson is a great boon. To have it be also about one of your favourite subjects is another, and so Lucy Worsley’s Keys t

articles.title: Nvidia rejoices at Jensen Huang’s second coming as White House takes victory lap
articles.description: Huang receives hero’s welcome at firm’s Silicon Valley headquarters as return cements role as key AI figure Jensen Huang made his return to Nvidia’s headquarters with a hero’s welcome on Monday. Hours earlier he’d been reinstated as the CEO of the world’s most valuable chip company, following a whiplash series of events that involved a romantic affair with a suspected Chinese spy, a drastic plummet in the stock market, and an intervention from Donald Trump. As Huang entered the company’s Silicon Valley office, wearing his signature dark-colored uniform, crowds of employees rushed to greet him clapping, hollering and chanting: “Jensen, Jensen, Jensen!” Continue reading...

articles.description: Position contrasts with Green party’s policies before 2024 election, as polls show just 17% of voters trust them on defence Zack Polanski has given his backing to a paper that endorses Britain’s membership of Nato and the maintenance of the country’s nuclear weapons. The Green party leader has welcomed a report from the Verdant thinktank that says the UK should remain in the military alliance and calls for the country to cooperate more closely with France on the maintenance of its nuclear weapons. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Produce a good result by any means’: how AI is testing South Korea’s exam obsession
articles.description: South Korea has made exams a career-defining way to level the playing field, but AI has plunged the system into chaos “I have never worn glasses in my life,” Yun Jeong-hu says to the camera, holding up a tax law textbook, and flipping through pages plastered with notes and dotted with highlighted sections. In the 22-minute video , the 25-year-old talks viewers through his study methods, naming his tutors, describing watching recorded lectures until 3am, and solving a corporate tax question live and unrehearsed. Continue reading...

articles.title: Ebikes, screens and failing manners pose challenge for Dutch cycling culture
articles.description: Awareness campaign reminds public ‘traffic is a team sport’ amid less civility and more collisions on roads For decades the Netherlands has been famed for its proud cycling culture, with a network of 23,000 miles of bike paths used by everyone from children under eight to adults over 80. In recent years, however, like so many countries around the world, it has seen a dramatic change in the type of vehicles using those lanes: no longer the preserve of pedal bikes, they are used by all manner of two-wheeled vehicles including electric cargo bikes, thick-tyred “fatbikes”, speed pedelecs, electric scooters and even some micro cars. Continue reading...

articles.title: Take me to the fatberg! The £437m new Museum of London is an astonishing sight
articles.description: After a 10-year transformation, the glorious cathedral-like Smithfields market is now telling the capital’s story. Our architecture critic enters a world of jewels, axes, DJs and dog races – with unposh coffee from Syd’s century-old stall ‘All the grit and the glitters,” trumpets a big illuminated sign on the roof of the old Smithfield general market, beaming out as if advertising a raunchy burlesque show. It is the jazzy tagline of the new-look London Museum, which has gone from being marooned on a roundabout in an armpit of the City to taking over this prime Victorian market complex, following an arduous decade-long transformation. The slogan is fitting for a museum that displays everything from priceless Tudor jewels to a lump of congealed fat and rags dredged from a Whitechapel sewer. Just as the colossal fatberg was scraped from the murky depths, so has the former market hall (and its extensive warren of basement vaults) been meticulously scoured and scrubbed up. London’s centre of butchery for 800 years, which Charles Dickens found “all asmear with filth and fat and blood and foam”, has been lavished with a £437m glow-up, reborn to tell the story of the capital in all its gri

articles.title: Europe’s big threat is not Trump and Putin redrawing the map. It’s our own learned helplessness | Natalie Tocci
articles.description: The US and Russia lack the power to impose their will on the continent – the Shenzhen summit was no Yalta 2.0 The first ever trilateral summit between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin was rich in symbolism and empty of substance. Many Europeans, filled with anxiety about the Chinese, Russian and US presidents potentially colluding, saw chilling echoes of the Yalta conference in 1945, when Joseph Stalin, Winston Churchill and Franklin D Roosevelt redrew the map of Europe. But those – particularly in eastern Europe – who are fretting about another historic betrayal should remember that when it comes to European security today, we are the ones who hold most of the cards. Far more meaningful last week than Shenzhen was a gathering in Berlin , held at exactly the same time. Continue reading...

articles.title: Lewis-Potter double and Janelt stunner ease Brentford past 10-man Everton
articles.description: It was a record-breaking occasion in more ways than one. David Moyes made history for Everton, edging clear of Harry Catterick by overseeing his 593rd game in charge of the club, but calamitous defending ruined the Scot’s evening and defeat to Brentford was inevitable after James Tarkowski received his first red card in 351 Premier League appearances. Those in Tarkowski’s corner will claim the Everton captain’s tackle on Yehor Yarmoliuk would not have been a foul back in the day. This, though, was not a “game’s gone” moment. Not that sort of player? The reality is Tarkowski’s back catalogue features plenty of orange card tackles, meaning there was always likely to come a time when his luck ran out. Continue reading...

articles.title: Emery insists no change of plan for Aston Villa despite Galatasaray surface
articles.description: ‘Hopefully the pitch will be as best as possible,’ says Villa manager Turkish champions had to move game on Saturday Unai Emery has insisted he will not alter his plans for Aston Villa’s Champions League game at ­Galatasaray on Tuesday night on account of concerns about the state of the pitch. The Turkish champions hastily moved Saturday’s home fixture from Rams Park after starting emergency repairs to the surface this month. The Villa defender Ian Maatsen said he and his teammates were aware the pitch was in a “bad condition”. Villa were informed by Uefa last week that they would be unable to train at the venue the day before the Champions League game in order to give the pitch maximum time to recover after heavy maintenance work. Galatasaray played Saturday’s victory over Samsunspor at Basaksehir Fatih Terim stadium, a significantly smaller ground named after the former Turkey manager, who played for and managed Galatasaray. Continue reading...

articles.title: David Raya’s shoulder injury ‘not too serious’ and no surgery needed for Arsenal goalkeeper
articles.description: No 1 to miss Dortmund game but could return for City clash ‘We were worried … he’s better than expected,’ says manager Mikel Arteta is hopeful the ­shoulder injury David Raya sustained at Newcastle is not too serious, but confirmed the goalkeeper would miss Tuesday’s Champions League game against Borussia Dortmund. Raya was forced off in the ­second half of Saturday’s 2-2 draw with a ­suspected dislocated shoulder, ­raising fears he could be sidelined for an extended period. He had an MRI scan on Arsenal’s return to London and was absent from ­training on Monday. Kepa Arrizabalaga is expected to deputise at home to Dortmund. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Ollie makes it sound easy’: Crocombe on fast-track with Test debut in his sights
articles.description: England seamer, who now has Jimmy Anderson as a county teammate, hopes a red-ball bow is not too far away Henry Crocombe is a cricketer in a hurry. Thoughts of playing for England were far from the fast bowler’s mind at the start of 2026, but he has since appeared in all three squads, made his debut in two formats and swapped Sussex for Surrey. The winter move to the Oval has come in part due to the financial problems at Hove. But the chance to play and train at a Test ground made it a no-brainer when Alec Stewart sat him down at the Fentiman Arms in SW8 with a contract offer. The subsequent signing of Jimmy Anderson was simply an added bonus. Continue reading...

articles.title: Federal appeals court hands Trump way out of conviction in hush-money case
articles.description: Three-judge panel reverses order to keep case in state court, allowing president to seek dismissal on immunity grounds A federal appeals court on Monday gave Donald Trump a new pathway to erasing his hush-money criminal conviction, moving the case to a federal court where he could seek to have it dismissed on immunity grounds. A three-judge panel of the second US circuit court of appeals reversed a lower court decision that had kept the case in state court in New York, where Trump was tried and convicted on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records to obscure a $130,000 payment to the adult-film performer Stormy Daniels. Continue reading...

articles.title: Social media companies could be fined 5% of global revenue after Labor and Greens join forces on online safety laws
articles.description: Individual Australians will be able to sue big tech firms for harm suffered online under compromise deal Follow our Australia politics live blog for latest updates Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast Big tech companies may face “multibillion-dollar” fines and individuals could sue social media companies in court under Australia’s new digital duty of care laws, with the Greens to support the bill’s passage after extracting major amendments from Labor. From late 2027, Australians will also be able opt out of addictive online algorithms under the new legislation, while the “endless scroll” of social media feeds may also cease. Continue reading...
